6740.text: In Ps.109.10 the operation 'wander about' (H5128, role-T3) is performed by 'his children' and directed outward (no fixed object, aimless roaming), immediately followed by the seeking (H1875) of food -- the same party (the children) both wanders and seeks, the wandering being the means by which the futile seeking is carried out.

6741.text: In Eccl.1.13 the operation 'applied' (H5414H, role-T3, 'applied my heart') is initiated by the speaker (Qoheleth) and directed toward his own heart/mind as the instrument, immediately followed by the seeking (H1875) and searching -- the speaker initiates both the application and the seeking upon himself.

6742.text: In Ps.109.10 M21 (beg, H7592) co-occurs with seeking (H1875): begging and seeking food are parallel destitution-acts performed by the same wandering children -- the two characteristics jointly depict total dispossession rather than one causing the other.

6743.text: In Eccl.1.13 M47 (heart, H3820A) and M16 (wisdom, H2451) co-occur; seeking (H1875) is the verb governing both -- the heart is the seeking party's faculty and wisdom is the means/manner of the search, making seeking the operative link joining an inner faculty to an epistemic method.

6769.text: In Deut.22.2 'seeks' (of a brother seeking his lost property) matches sense 1a2/1a5, a straightforward literal-search use with no shift from base gloss.

6772.text: In 2Chr.26.5, H1875 occurs twice ('seek'/'sought' God) alongside M15 (instructed) and M46 (prosper). First pass: darash names Uzziah's sustained active pursuit of God, which M15 (Zechariah's instruction) enables and M46 (prospering) results from -- seeking functions as the causal hinge between instruction received and prosperity granted.

6773.text: In Deut.22.2, H1875 ('seeks') is the only M-code characteristic present in the verse.

6774.text: In Ps.14.2, H1875 ('seek') co-occurs with M16 (understand). First pass: darash names the culminating act the Lord looks for -- understanding (M16) is presented as the necessary prior condition/companion of true seeking; the two are paired as a single ideal (one who understands AND seeks God), with darash naming the outward-turned pursuit and M16 the inward comprehension enabling it.

6775.text: Ps.53.2 parallels Ps.14.2: H1875 ('seek') co-occurs with M16 (understand); darash again names the pursuit paired with, and completing, the understanding named by M16.

6777.text: In Amos.5.5, H1875 ('seek', prohibited toward Bethel) co-occurs with M58 (come to nothing). First pass: darash names the forbidden cultic pursuit of Bethel, and M58 names its worthless outcome -- the seeking itself is condemned as directed at an object destined for nullity, linking the act to its futile object.

6780.text: In Job.7.21, H7836 ('seek') itself is not tagged role-T3 in the role list; no operation-tagged word is paired with a party tag co-occurring with H7836 in this verse to establish a D7.7.1 relation.

6782.text: In 2Chr.26.5, H1875 is tagged M83, not T3; no role-T3 tag attaches to either occurrence of 'seek/sought' in this verse's role list.

6783.text: In Deut.22.2, H1875 ('seeks') is tagged M83 only, not role-T3; no T3 tag is attached to it, so no D7.7.1 relation is established from this word.

6784.text: In Jer.21.2, H1875 ('Inquire') is tagged M83 only, not role-T3; no D7.7.1 relation applies from this word directly.

6799.text: In Job.7.21, 'seek' (shachar) reverses its usual direction: normally the human seeks God diligently, but here Job envisions God seeking him diligently after death -- a poignant, ironic inversion of the base gloss's typical worshipper-toward-deity direction, since Job will already be gone ('I shall not be'), making the diligent search futile. This is a notable contextual nuance beyond the plain base sense.

6821.text: In 2Chr.17.3 'seek the Baals' uses H1875 in its devotional-seeking sense (1a3b, seeking heathen deities) as a negated contrast to seeking the Lord -- squarely within the base gloss of devotional/cultic seeking, applied here negatively to idols.

6822.text: In Job.3.4 'may God ... not seek it' applies H1875 metaphorically to God's non-regard of a day, extending the 'seek/care for' sense (1a8, seek with care) to a poetic wish that the day be utterly disregarded -- a figurative extension within the base sense rather than a distinct nuance.

6823.text: In Isa.65.10 'sought me' uses H1875 in its devotional sense (seeking God), consistent with the base gloss, describing the covenant people's faithful pursuit of God.

6824.text: In Jer.29.7 'seek the welfare of the city' extends H1875 to seeking a civic good/outcome rather than a person -- still within the broad base sense of earnest pursuit/care but applied to an abstract communal object (shalom) rather than a deity or individual, a natural extension without a distinct new sense.

6828.text: In 2Chr.12.14 'seek the Lord' uses the devotional sense, negated to explain Rehoboam's evil as failure of heart-set devotional pursuit of God -- within the base gloss.

6831.text: In 2Chr.17.3, H1875 (seeking, negated toward Baals) sits alongside M76 (ways, H1870, Jehoshaphat's walking in his father's earlier ways) -- the seeking-characteristic and the ways-characteristic are tightly related: Jehoshaphat's fidelity is expressed as walking in right ways AND not seeking false gods, two complementary facets of covenant loyalty in the same verse.

6832.text: No other M-code characteristic co-occurs in Job.3.4 besides H1875 itself; the verse's other tagged words are role-T2/T3/T5 grammatical markers, not M-code characteristics.

6833.text: In Isa.65.10, H1875 (the people who sought God) co-occurs with M33 (H7258, lie down/resting place) describing herds' rest -- the two M-codes describe different subjects (God-seeking people vs. resting livestock) in a shared pastoral-restoration image; no direct conceptual connection between the seeking-characteristic and the resting-characteristic beyond shared setting.

6834.text: In Jer.29.7, H1875 (seek the welfare) is tightly bound to M33 (welfare/shalom, H7965) as its direct object, and also co-occurs with M42 (pray, H6419) -- seeking and praying are paired as complementary devotional-civic acts, both directed toward securing the city's shalom, with H1875 supplying the active-pursuit half of the pairing.

6838.text: In 2Chr.12.14, H1875 (seek the Lord, negated) is tightly related to M24/M58 (evil, H7451) and M23/M47 (set the heart, H3559/H3820) -- the verse causally links failure to set the heart to seek the Lord with the doing of evil, making H1875's negated seeking the direct explanatory cause of the evil-characteristic's manifestation.

6841.text: In 2Chr.17.3, H1875 ('seek') is negated: Jehoshaphat is the initiator who does NOT direct this seeking-operation toward the Baals, contrasted implicitly with directing devotion toward the Lord instead.

6842.text: In Job.3.4, H1875 ('seek') is negated with God as the withheld initiator: God is asked not to direct seeking-regard toward 'that day', a wish that the day be excluded from divine attention.

6843.text: In Isa.65.10, H1875 ('sought') has 'my people' as initiators directing the seeking-operation toward God ('me'), describing the restored covenant people's pursuit of the Lord.

6844.text: In Jer.29.7, H1875 ('seek') is an imperative: the exiles (party addressed) are commanded by the Lord (through Jeremiah) to initiate seeking directed toward the welfare of the city of exile.

6848.text: In 2Chr.12.14, H1875 ('seek') is negated: Rehoboam is the initiator who failed to direct seeking toward the Lord, explaining his evil conduct.

6878.text: In Isa.65.10 'lie down' (rebets, as construct noun for a resting place for herds) is used in its base sense of a place of repose for animals -- squarely within the base gloss.

6893.text: In Deut.23.6, Ps.34.10, 2Chr.16.12, and Isa.9.13 darash sits within its base sense of seeking/inquiring of a person, deity, or welfare -- no notable divergence from the general gloss.

6894.text: Deut.23.6: darash ('seek') governs the object 'peace/prosperity' (M33/M05/M18-tagged terms) -- the seeking-characteristic here operates as the withheld-action toward another people's wellbeing, showing this characteristic as the vehicle that carries or denies the wellbeing-characteristic to its object.

6895.text: Ps.34.10: those who 'seek' (darash) the Lord are contrasted with lack of 'good' (M05/M18) -- seeking functions as the condition that secures possession of the good-characteristic; the seeking-act is causally prior to the good outcome.

6896.text: 2Chr.16.12: Asa's disease (M73) is set against his failure to 'seek' the Lord -- the seeking-characteristic's absence is diagnosed as morally/spiritually contributory to reliance on physicians rather than God; seeking here functions as the missing remedy alongside physical affliction.

6898.text: Deut.23.6: darash is an Israelite-initiated operation ('you shall not seek') directed toward the Ammonite/Moabite party's peace and prosperity -- forbidding the initiating party from extending goodwill toward the named other party.

6899.text: Ps.34.10: the operation is initiated by 'those who seek' (worshippers) and directed toward the Lord as party -- an upward-directed devotional pursuit.

6900.text: 2Chr.16.12: Asa (party) is the (negated) initiator of the seek-operation, which would have been directed toward the Lord (party) but instead was redirected to physicians -- the operation's proper divine target is bypassed.

6918.text: In Rom.3.11, Heb.11.6, and 1Pet.1.10 ekzeteo sits within its base sense of diligent/earnest seeking -- no notable divergence from the general gloss.

6919.text: Heb.11.6: ekzeteo ('seek him') operates alongside faith (M13) and belief (M19) as the culminating relational act -- faith is the precondition, belief in God's existence the content, and seeking-with-reward-expectation the resulting posture; this characteristic supplies the goal-directed, reward-oriented dimension that faith and belief presuppose.

6921.text: 1Pet.1.10: ekzeteo ('searched') is the prophets' response to salvation (M79) and grace (M50), prophesied (M43) beforehand -- this characteristic names the diligent investigative activity the prophets undertook in response to the grace/salvation already announced to them, i.e. it is the human-side inquiry answering divine self-disclosure.

6923.text: Heb.11.6: the seek-operation is initiated by 'whoever would draw near' (the human party) and directed toward God (party) as the one who rewards.

6925.text: 1Pet.1.10: the prophets (party) initiate the search-operation directed toward the grace/salvation content revealed to believers (the recipient party, 'yours').

6954.text: In Ps.119.2, Ps.119.10, 2Chr.17.4, 2Chr.31.21 and 1Chr.13.3 darash carries its standard devotional sense of seeking God/His commandments wholeheartedly -- squarely within the base gloss, no divergence.

6955.text: No other M-code characteristic co-occurs with darash in 2Chr.31.9 or 1Chr.13.3 (both restricted to T-role co-tags).

6956.text: In 2Chr.31.21 M36 (service), M54 (law/commandments), and M46 (prospered) are co-present with seeking, but they describe surrounding acts of obedience and outcome rather than being conceptually fused with the act of seeking itself; seeking functions as the wholehearted disposition that undergirds but is distinct from the law-keeping and the prospering outcome.

6957.text: In Ps.119.2 M80 (blessed) and M74 (keep) co-occur with seeking; seeking is the relational counterpart to keeping testimonies -- the blessed state results from both keeping and seeking together, but seeking itself remains a distinct act from the disposition of keeping.

6958.text: In Ps.119.10 M47 (heart) and M76 (wander) are present; seeking with the whole heart stands in direct tension with wandering from the commandments -- seeking functions as the guarding orientation that prevents the wandering named by the co-occurring M-code.

6959.text: In Ps.78.34 M11/M81 (repented) co-occurs with two seeking-verbs (darash and shachar); seeking here occupies the positive-response pole triggered by judgment, paired with repentance as the accompanying inward turn -- seeking is the outward-directed act, repentance the inward corollary.

6960.text: No other M-code characteristic co-occurs with darash in 2Chr.17.4 beyond M54 (commandments); seeking God and walking in commandments are presented as parallel but separately-coded acts, with seeking as the root orientation from which commandment-keeping follows.

6975.text: In Prov.7.15 shachar's sense of eager seeking is used in a negative seductive context, but this is the natural range of the term (object-neutral intensity) rather than a genuine divergence from its base gloss.

6976.text: In Ps.78.34 shachar sits within its base gloss of earnest seeking, paired with darash for intensification -- no additional divergence beyond the expected devotional sense.

6977.text: In Ps.78.34, darash (H1875, same cluster) and M11/M81 (repented) co-occur with shachar; from shachar's own vantage the eager-intensity pursuit sits alongside darash's more general seeking as a rhetorical doubling (seeking...sought earnestly), while repentance remains the separate inward-turning act that darash's pass already covers.

6978.text: In Prov.7.15 M02/M50 (co-tagged on 'you'/face) is present but is a party-reference tag on the object of pursuit, not a separate characteristic conceptually interacting with the eager-seeking act; no meaningful M-code relation to record beyond the direct object relation.

6992.text: Mark.1.36 is this word's sole NT occurrence, and its use ('searched for him') matches the base stepGloss ('look for, search for') exactly with no distinguishing shift; there is no other occurrence to compare against.

6993.text: No other M-code characteristic co-occurs with katadiokō in Mark.1.36; the verse's other tagged words carry only T-role (party/connector) codes.

6994.text: The operation word 'searched' (G2614, role-T3-equivalent operation verb) is initiated by Simon and his companions (parties) and directed toward Jesus ('him') -- a party-to-party search operation with Jesus as the sought target.

7012.text: In Job.39.8 darash describes a wild donkey's searching after green pasture — an animal/physical sense fully within the base gloss's range (to seek diligently), not a distinct nuance shift; the term's flexibility to cover both animal foraging and religious enquiry is inherent to its base semantic range, not a divergence.

7013.text: 2Chr.34.3's use of darash (seek God) sits squarely within the base gloss's religious/devotional sense (1a3a) with no notable nuance shift from the term's other occurrences of seeking God.

7014.text: Job.5.8's 'I would seek God' matches the base gloss's sense of consulting/appealing to God in crisis; no divergence beyond the standard religious enquiry sense.

7015.text: Ps.119.45's 'I have sought your precepts' fits the base gloss's sense of seeking/enquiring with application (1a7), consistent with its use in v.94; no distinguishing nuance beyond standard devotional seeking.

7016.text: Ps.119.94 repeats the identical construction and sense as Ps.119.45 ('sought your precepts'), no additional nuance beyond the base gloss.

7017.text: 2Chr.34.3 also contains M63/M72 (reign) and M12 (purge/cleanse) and M55 (carved image). Seeking God here is the initiating spiritual act that precedes and motivates the later cultic purge (M12) and stands apart from the royal reign timeframe (M63/M72) and the idols being removed (M55) — seeking functions as the causal root of the reform narrative, not merely coincidental with these other M-codes.

7018.text: Job.5.8 also contains M16 (cause, H1700) and M15 (commit, H7760H). Seeking God here is presented as the prerequisite act to committing one's cause to Him — seeking establishes the relationship within which the cause (M16) can then be entrusted (M15); the three are sequential rather than overlapping in function.

7019.text: No other M-code characteristic is present in Job.39.8 alongside searches (H1875).

7020.text: Ps.119.45 also contains M08 (wide place, H7342H). The wide place is the resultant condition of walking freely, not something sought directly by darash; seeking precepts is the ground and cause of the freedom described, but the two M-codes describe distinct elements (act of seeking vs. resulting spaciousness).

7021.text: Ps.119.94 also contains M45 (save, H3467). The plea to be saved and the report of having sought precepts stand as complementary but distinct actions — seeking is the ground of belonging ('I am yours') that undergirds the appeal for salvation, but the two verbs describe different relational moves (past-completed seeking vs. present imperative plea).

7022.text: In 2Chr.34.3, the operation-tagged word 'began' (H2490C, role-T3) is directed at 'seek' (H1875) — the party (Josiah, 'he') initiates the seeking-action toward the God of David his father; a second 'began' likewise initiates the purge (H2891) toward the high places/idols. Seeking-God is the operation's first object, purge follows as its consequence.

7023.text: No role-T3 operation word co-occurs with a party tag alongside H1875 in Job.5.8, Job.39.8, Ps.119.45, or Ps.119.94 in this batch's role lists (the seeking verb itself is not additionally tagged role-T3, and no separate T3-tagged operation word with a party target is present).

7036.text: Job.24.5's 'seeking game' sits squarely within the base gloss's sense of diligent/earnest seeking (Piel), with no notable nuance shift — the physical foraging use matches the term's expected semantic domain.

7037.text: No other M-code characteristic is present in Job.24.5 alongside 'seeking' (H7836); the surrounding vocabulary (wild donkeys, desert, toil, game, wasteland, food, children) carries no other M-code tag in this batch.

7038.text: In Job.24.5, the role-T3 operation word 'go out' (H3318G) is initiated by the party 'the poor' and directed toward their toil, with the participle 'seeking' (H7836) further specifying that departure's purpose — the poor go out toward game/prey, showing the operation and the seeking-act converge on the same directional target (securing food).

7049.text: G2212 (zeteo) is the semantically widest member of the cluster, covering everything from literal physical search to hostile pursuit-to-kill to devotional seeking of God/the kingdom; its NT occurrences show the term's moral valence is supplied entirely by grammatical object and context rather than by the verb itself.

7051.text: epizeteo (G1934) is attested in classical Greek from Herodotus onward across administrative, investigative, and demand senses; its NT usage narrows to a recurring idiom of demanding a sign from Jesus, plus broader senses of anxious pursuit of provisions and eschatological longing for a homeland.

7052.text: katadiokō occurs only once in the NT (Mark.1.36), used benignly of the disciples searching for Jesus; its classical/LXX attestations (Thucydides, LXX Ps.17.38) show a base sense of close/hostile pursuit, so this single NT occurrence is a narrowed, non-hostile application of an otherwise intensive-pursuit verb.

7053.text: baqash's idiom 'seek the life/soul' (e.g. Ps.38.12, 2Sam.4.8, Prov.29.10, Jer.4.30, Jer.11.21) consistently means 'seek to kill', a lethal-hostile-pursuit sense sharply diverging from the term's more neutral or devotional occurrences (e.g. 2Chr.15.13 'seek the Lord'), showing the root's moral valence is entirely determined by its grammatical object.

7055.text: shachar's semantic range is narrower and more intensively focused than baqash or darash, concentrated almost entirely on 'diligent/early/earnest' seeking -- most frequently of God (Ps.63.1, Isa.26.9, Prov.8.17) but also of prey/food (Job.24.5) or a seductive target (Prov.7.15) -- its moral neutrality (like baqash's) is set by object, but its distinguishing feature vs. the other two Hebrew roots is the added connotation of urgency/priority tied etymologically to 'dawn'.

7056.text: G1567 (ekzeteo) and G1934 (epizeteo) both intensify the base zeteo root via a directional prefix (ek- 'out/thoroughly' vs epi- 'upon/toward'), and both share the same semantic split visible cross-strong: a devotional/diligent-seeking sense (ekzeteo: Acts.15.17, Heb.11.6, Rom.3.11, 1Pet.1.10; epizeteo: Heb.11.14, Heb.13.14, Acts.13.7) alongside a demanding/legal-exaction sense (ekzeteo: Luke.11.50-51, blood 'required'; epizeteo: Matt.12.39, Matt.16.4, Mark.8.12, Luke.11.29, demanding a sign; Acts.19.39, formal legal matter). Both Greek terms thus independently develop the same two-pole range (earnest seeking <-> exacting demand) from the same simple root, making them the closest pair in this subgroup.

7057.text: G1934 (epizeteo) shares with G1567 (ekzeteo) the same two-pole range: devotional/aspirational seeking (Heb.11.14 homeland, Heb.13.14 city to come, Rom.11.7 status Israel failed to obtain) versus demanding/exacting (Matt.12.39, Matt.16.4, Mark.8.12, Luke.11.29 demanding a sign; Acts.19.39 legal matter to be settled). Where ekzeteo's demand-sense is judicial/retributive (blood exacted), epizeteo's demand-sense is typically a testing or procedural request (a sign demanded from Jesus, a legal matter raised in assembly) -- a real difference in the character of what is 'demanded,' not merely a synonym overlap.

7058.text: H7836 (shachar) shares the subgroup's general 'intensive/earnest seeking' theme with G1567/G1934 conceptually (both Greek terms and shachar converge on devotional 'seek God/wisdom diligently' senses: shachar in Ps.63.1, Isa.26.9, Job.8.5, Prov.8.17, Ps.78.34 parallels ekzeteo in Acts.15.17/Heb.11.6/Rom.3.11 and epizeteo's aspirational uses), but there is no lexical or morphological relationship -- shachar is a distinct Hebrew root (tied etymologically to 'dawn/early') with no direct Greek cognate among this subgroup's members, and unlike ekzeteo/epizeteo it never carries a judicial 'demand an account/blood' sense; its 'demanding' pole (Job.7.21, God seeking Job) is ironic-reversal rather than legal exaction.

7059.text: Cross-strong, the two Greek members (ekzeteo, epizeteo) both attest a passive/legal-exaction voice pattern absent from shachar entirely: ekzeteo's future/aorist passive 'will be required/may be charged' (Luke.11.50-51) and epizeteo's passive-adjacent 'is matter of question/demand' senses in LSJ have no shachar counterpart -- shachar occurs only in Qal/Piel active-voice forms across all 12 occurrences, meaning the Hebrew member of this subgroup carries no attested passive 'held-to-account' construction, unlike its two Greek subgroup-mates.

7060.text: Within the subgroup's shared 'intensification of the base seek-root' logic, ekzeteo's intensifying element (ek-, 'out/thoroughly') most naturally supports a completion/exhaustiveness reading (searching OUT fully, exacting an account IN FULL -- e.g. 'from the foundation of the world,' Luke.11.50), whereas epizeteo's intensifying element (epi-, 'upon/toward/further') most naturally supports a directedness/insistence reading (pressing TOWARD an object, seeking FURTHER/again -- LSJ's 'seek for besides,' 'inquire further'). Both belong to this subgroup's 'thoroughness or added directedness' core description, but each realizes a different half of it: ekzeteo leans toward thoroughness, epizeteo toward directedness/insistence.

7061.text: Epizeteo's four 'demanding a sign' occurrences (Matt.12.39, Matt.16.4, Mark.8.12, Luke.11.29) form a single tight cluster sharing one idiom -- 'this evil/adulterous generation seeks/demands a sign' -- functioning as a fixed Synoptic controversy formula rather than four independently-nuanced uses; this is the strong's own largest verse-grouping and is the clearest place where epizeteo's 'demand' sense (rather than its 'aspire/long for' sense) is activated.

7062.text: Ekzeteo's occurrence in Heb.12.17 (Esau's tearful, failed, retrospective seeking of a forfeited blessing) has no parallel anywhere in epizeteo's or shachar's occurrence lists in this subgroup -- neither other member attests a 'seeking too late, after disqualification, and failing' sense; epizeteo's closest analog (Rom.11.7, Israel 'failed to obtain what it was seeking') is corporate/covenantal rather than personal/emotional, and shachar's occurrences of failed seeking (Prov.1.28, Job.7.21) involve either wisdom's refusal to answer or death forestalling the search, not repentance foreclosed by an irreversible past act -- making Heb.12.17 a distinctive, non-overlapping sense within the subgroup.

7063.text: Shachar's occurrence in Prov.11.27 ('diligently seeks good...but evil comes to him who searches for it') stands alongside its cluster-sibling H1245 (baqash) within the very same verse, forming an intra-verse doublet of intensive-seeking terms -- this pairing (also seen with H1875 darash alongside shachar in Ps.78.34, and H1245 alongside shachar in Hos.5.15) shows the Hebrew seeking-vocabulary routinely stacks multiple intensive roots together for rhetorical emphasis, a stacking pattern not seen between the two Greek members (ekzeteo and epizeteo never co-occur in the same verse in this occurrence set).

7064.text: Unlike both Greek members, whose intensifying force comes from a prefix added to a plainer root (zeteo), shachar's intensifying force is inherent to the lexeme itself (traditionally linked to the noun for 'dawn,' i.e. built-in urgency/earliness rather than compounded prepositional intensification) -- so the subgroup's 'intensive/exhaustive seeking' label is achieved by two different linguistic mechanisms: Greek compounding (ek-/epi- + zeteo) versus a single Hebrew root whose own core meaning already encodes earliness/earnestness.

7065.text: As the sole member strong of C_hostile_pursuit, G2614 (katadiōkō) has no other subgroup member to compare against for shared or divergent meaning; the cross-strong synergy this stage targets cannot be performed within this subgroup -- the comparison is necessarily null, not a finding of similarity or difference.

7066.text: G2614's own full occurrence list (corpus-wide) is a single NT instance, but its lexical range attested in the meaning sources (LSJ, strong_meaning_tree) spans hostile military pursuit (Thucydides), LXX overdriving of cattle (Gen.33.13), metaphorical striving to attain (Polybius), and non-hostile personal search (Mark.1.36 -- disciples seeking Jesus). Within this subgroup labeled 'hostile pursuit', the only NT-attested sense is explicitly benign, so the strong's placement here rests on its etymological/attested-range capacity for hostile pursuit rather than on its actual NT occurrence, which is neutral-to-positive in tone.

7067.text: Morphology of the sole occurrence (V-AAI-3S, aorist active indicative) shows the subjects (Simon and companions) actively performing the search themselves -- an agent-initiated act, not something done to them nor caused by them in another. No voice/stem variation exists across occurrences to compare (only one instance), so no meaning-relevant distinction can be drawn from morph variation within this strong; this is recorded as a genuine no-distinction-found result given the single-occurrence corpus.

7073.text: Across this pass's 'inquire' surface-form cluster (1Kgs.22.8, 2Chr.18.7, 2Kgs.22.13/2Chr.34.21, 2Kgs.3.11, 2Kgs.1.2/1.3/1.6/1.16, 2Kgs.8.8, 1Kgs.14.5, Ezek.20.3, 1Sam.28.7, Jer.10.21, Gen.25.22, Exod.18.15, Deut.12.30, 1Sam.9.9, 1Kgs.22.7/2Chr.18.6, 2Kgs.22.18/2Chr.34.26, Isa.8.19, Jer.37.7, 2Chr.32.31, Isa.19.3, Zeph.1.6, Isa.11.10, Ezek.20.1, 1Chr.21.30, Isa.9.13) the term consistently denotes formal consultation of a deity or authoritative source (the Lord, a prophet, an oracle, Baal-zebub, mediums/necromancers) for a verdict or answer -- the single largest and most cohesive sense-cluster in H1875's full occurrence set, matching this subgroup's core description of institutional/cultic resort to authority for guidance.

7074.text: The 'Seek' surface form in this pass (Amos.5.4/5.6/5.14, 1Chr.16.11, Ps.105.4, Isa.55.6, Isa.34.16) is used almost exclusively in imperative form as an urgent devotional/covenantal exhortation ('Seek the LORD/his strength/good and live') rather than as narrative report of consultation -- a distinct sub-mode of this subgroup's formal-inquiry sense: exhortation to habitual, life-orienting seeking of God rather than a single act of consulting an oracle for a specific verdict.

7076.text: The 'inquired'/'seeking'/'searched' occurrences in this pass show the root's outer boundary away from formal cultic consultation: Lev.10.16 (procedural cultic checking of a sacrifice), 2Sam.11.3 (mundane social inquiry about a woman's identity), Jer.38.4/2Chr.31.21 (civic/devotional 'seeking welfare' or 'seeking God' as ongoing disposition), Ps.109.10 (destitute foraging for food), Ezek.34.8 (pastoral searching for lost sheep), and Judg.6.29 (forensic investigation of who committed a deed) -- these occurrences share the base sense of careful, purposeful inquiry but apply it to secular, pastoral, or forensic objects rather than deity/oracle consultation, showing the root's flexibility extends the subgroup's core 'formal consultation' sense outward to any object warranting diligent investigation.

7081.text: Ezek.34.6 and Ezek.34.11 both use 'search' of shepherding care for scattered sheep -- one negated (no shepherd searches) and one emphatic (God himself will search) -- forming a matched pair where the pastoral-care sense of darash is activated on both the human failure side and the divine remedy side of the same extended shepherd metaphor.

7082.text: 1Chr.26.31's 'search' (Niphal, 'search was made') applies darash to an administrative genealogical/military census-investigation rather than the more common cultic-consultation or pastoral-care senses -- a bureaucratic/institutional nuance distinct from both Ezek.34's shepherding sense and the religious-inquiry sense dominant elsewhere in this pass's surface forms.

7083.text: Deut.4.29's 'search' pairs darash with baqash (H1245, this subgroup's sole other member's absence notwithstanding -- here baqash appears in-verse though as a different subgroup's home strong) in an intensive doublet urging wholehearted covenantal seeking of God -- matching the devotional-seeking pole already well attested for this strong.

7084.text: Isa.16.5's 'seeks' (participle, 'one who...seeks justice') applies darash to an abstract ethical/judicial object (justice, mishpat) rather than a person or deity -- the ruler's habitual disposition of pursuing justice, distinct from the more common person-or-deity-directed senses.

7085.text: Prov.31.13's 'seeks' (wool and flax) applies darash to mundane domestic-industrious acquisition of material goods -- a base, non-cultic, non-forensic use showing the term's range extends to ordinary diligent labor, distinct from its dominant devotional/consultative register elsewhere.

7086.text: Lam.3.25's 'seeks him' (the Lord) sits within the devotional base sense of darash, paralleling other 'seek the Lord' occurrences; no divergence from the established pattern of this strong's core covenantal-seeking usage.

7087.text: Deut.22.2's 'seeks' applies darash to a lost-property scenario (a brother seeking his lost animal/object) -- a plain literal-search sense with no cultic or judicial overtone, showing this strong's semantic floor extends to everyday recovery of possessions alongside its higher religious/legal registers.

7091.text: 1Chr.28.9, Prov.11.27, and Job.39.8 all render darash as 'searches' but span three distinct registers: God searching all hearts (devotional-omniscient), a person searching for evil (moral-negative object), and a wild animal searching for pasture (literal/animal). This triad illustrates the verb's semantic elasticity across divine, moral, and mundane subjects within one surface form.

7093.text: Ps.10.13 and Ps.10.15 both render darash as legal-accountability terms ('call to account'/'account') within the same psalm, applying the forensic-demand sense of darash to God's judicial reckoning with the wicked -- consistent with the Gen.9.5/Gen.42.22 'reckoning' pattern but here directed at moral wickedness rather than bloodshed specifically.

7103.text: 1Chr.28.8's 'seek out' and Job.10.6's 'search for' both apply darash to an investigative-demand sense with a specific object -- commandments to be diligently observed versus iniquity being probed by God -- showing the same surface form covers both covenant-positive diligence and divine-forensic scrutiny.

7111.text: Where the subgroup's seeking is directed toward God/wisdom, it reveals a belief that the sought one exists, rewards, or can be found (Heb.11.6 'believe that he exists and that he rewards'; Prov.8.17 'those who seek me diligently find me'; Ps.63.1). Where it is directed toward a sign or an account (Matt.12.39/16.4, Luke.11.50-51), it reveals unbelief or a demand for proof/accountability rather than settled belief. In Heb.12.17 Esau's seeking reveals a late realization/perception that what was lost cannot be regained.

7112.text: Both patterns occur. In devotional occurrences the seeking follows a prior belief (Heb.11.6 -- one must first 'believe that he exists' before seeking him for reward), while in penitential occurrences (Hos.5.15, Ps.78.34) seeking follows judgment/distress and produces or confirms acknowledgment of guilt. In judicial occurrences (Luke.11.50-51) the 'seeking/requiring' itself constitutes the judgement (an act of holding accountable), so it does not precede a separate belief but enacts one.

7113.text: Several occurrences orient the seeker toward a future fullness not yet possessed: Heb.11.14 and Heb.13.14 speak of seeking a homeland/city 'that is to come'; Isa.26.9 links earnest seeking to a future in which the world's inhabitants 'learn righteousness' when God's judgments come. This forward-orientation frames the seeking-characteristic as pilgrim/eschatological rather than merely present-satisfying.

7116.text: Both are attested. Reversible: seeking that leads to finding and repentance (Prov.8.17, Ps.78.34) can be entered into or renewed. Irreversible: Esau's seeking in Heb.12.17 comes after a disqualifying act and 'he found no chance to repent' -- the door once closed cannot be reopened by any degree of subsequent earnest seeking, making that particular instance of the characteristic irreversible in its outcome though not in the seeking-act itself.

7119.text: In Ps.63.1 the felt quality is intense, bodily, and settled -- 'earnestly I seek you; my soul thirsts...my flesh faints' -- a whole-person longing rather than a passing impulse. In Heb.12.17 it is transient but acute -- 'sought it with tears', a burst of grief-driven desperation. In Matt.16.4 it is a demanding, testing posture rather than an emotion of longing.

7122.text: Yes. Ekzeteo/epizeteo's demanding sense operates through speech -- a spoken demand for a sign (Matt.12.39 'seeks for a sign', Mark.8.12, Luke.11.29) or a formally raised legal matter to be 'settled in the regular assembly' (Acts.19.39). Shachar's devotional sense in Hos.5.15/Job.8.5 pairs seeking with explicit speech-acts ('plead with the Almighty for mercy').

7125.text: In Rom.3.11 the person in whom seeking is characteristically absent is described as one who 'does not understand' -- an inner-being state of blindness/darkened understanding. In Heb.12.17 Esau, though he seeks with tears, is in a state of having 'found no chance to repent' -- the door is shut internally as well as circumstantially, so the seeking cannot take hold to produce repentance.

7133.text: The characteristic is shared, not merely analogical: God himself is shown seeking in Job.7.21 ('you will seek me, but I shall not be'), the mirror-image of the human seeking-of-God found throughout the subgroup (Ps.63.1, Prov.8.17). Both parties can occupy the seeking role, though with different outcomes and stakes.

7135.text: The pattern shows the characteristic engaging soul/spirit level pervasively (Ps.63.1 'my soul thirsts,' Isa.26.9 'my spirit within me earnestly seeks') and occasionally the body as an expressive overflow (Ps.63.1 'my flesh faints'), but the body link is expressive/indicative rather than causally central -- the body registers the intensity of the soul/spirit's seeking rather than itself seeking. The characteristic never engages a purely bodily mechanism independent of soul/spirit direction.

7136.text: Where a body link exists (Ps.63.1's 'flesh faints'), it runs from soul/spirit expressing through the body -- the flesh's fainting is downstream evidence of the soul's thirst, not an independent bodily initiator of the seeking. This means the physical symptom testifies to, rather than generates, the seeking-characteristic.

7153.text: Frequent co-occurring adjacent characteristics include: faith/belief (Heb.11.6, drawing near to God), understanding (Rom.3.11, paired negatively with seeking), love (Prov.8.17, Prov.13.24), repentance (Hos.5.15, Ps.78.34, Heb.12.17), guilt-acknowledgment (Hos.5.15), and hardening (Rom.11.7). Sign-demanding contexts co-occur with 'evil' and 'adulterous' descriptors of the generation (Matt.12.39, Matt.16.4, Luke.11.29).

7155.text: A recurring sequence: acknowledgment of guilt precedes seeking (Hos.5.15 'until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face'); belief precedes seeking (Heb.11.6, 'must believe...and that he rewards those who seek him'); seeking precedes finding (Prov.8.17 'seek me diligently find me'); and being killed/judged precedes repentance which accompanies seeking (Ps.78.34 'When he killed them, they sought him; they repented').

7157.text: Yes -- seeking produces finding, by the mechanism of diligent, sustained pursuit meeting a responsive object: 'those who seek me diligently find me' (Prov.8.17). It can also produce learned righteousness at a corporate scale when paired with divine judgment (Isa.26.9, 'when your judgments are in the earth, the inhabitants of the world learn righteousness').

7163.text: Where the characteristic operates devotionally (ekzeteo in Heb.11.6, Rom.3.11; epizeteo in Heb.11.14, Heb.13.14; shachar in Ps.63.1, Isa.26.9, Job.8.5, Prov.8.17), the seeker perceives God/wisdom/a homeland as real, attainable, and worth pursuing -- the act presupposes a prior belief that the object exists and rewards the seeker (explicit in Heb.11.6: 'must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him').

7164.text: Where the characteristic operates in the judicial/demanding register (ekzeteo in Luke.11.50-51; epizeteo in Matt.12.39, Matt.16.4, Mark.8.12, Luke.11.29), the party believes an account is owed or a proof required -- the demanding generation judges Jesus's claims insufficient without a sign, and divine justice judges 'this generation' answerable for accumulated bloodguilt.

7165.text: In Heb.12.17, Esau's seeking-with-tears reveals his belated conclusion that the blessing he forfeited was truly valuable and that he wished to reverse his own prior choice -- but the narrative discloses he perceives wrongly that the door remains open; his perception is contradicted by the outcome (no chance to repent).

7166.text: Across the verses, the characteristic follows a belief more often than it precedes one: Heb.11.6 makes belief in God's existence and rewarding character the explicit precondition for seeking; Hos.5.15 and Ps.78.34 show acknowledgment of guilt/repentance preceding the earnest seeking. In the demanding-sign occurrences, however, the seeking itself reveals an already-formed unbelieving judgment (the generation is 'evil and adulterous') rather than producing a new belief -- so the characteristic mostly follows or expresses prior belief/disposition rather than generating one, with the sign-demanding cases showing seeking as an expression of settled unbelief rather than a step toward belief.

7167.text: The subgroup shows clear future-fullness orientation: Heb.11.14 and Heb.13.14 (epizeteo) name a 'homeland' and 'city that is to come' not yet possessed; Acts.15.17 (ekzeteo) envisions Gentiles yet to seek the Lord eschatologically; Isa.26.9 (shachar) links earnest seeking to a future state when 'the inhabitants of the world learn righteousness.' The movement is consistently toward something the person does not yet have -- a not-yet-attained relational or covenantal completeness.

7168.text: The immediate response varies by context and register: it ranges from grief-driven urgency (Heb.12.17, tears), to bodily longing (Ps.63.1, thirst/faint; Isa.26.9, soul yearning), to hostile testing (Matt.16.4, demand for a sign), to calm ongoing pilgrim-orientation (Heb.11.14, Heb.13.14). There is no single uniform immediate response across the subgroup -- it is shaped entirely by whether the seeking is devotional, judicial, or testing.

7169.text: The immediate response is often emotionally charged and momentary (tears, testing demand, thirst), while the sustained effect the subgroup implies is either a lasting relational orientation (pilgrim-seeking of a homeland, Heb.11.14/13.14, sustained indefinitely) or a lasting negative verdict (Rom.11.7, Israel's sustained failure to obtain what it sought, followed by hardening). The sustained effect thus outlasts the initial emotional charge and settles into either an enduring posture (waiting/longing) or an enduring condition (hardened failure).

7170.text: The evidence shows both: Esau's forfeiture in Heb.12.17 is irreversible (his tearful seeking cannot undo the prior choice, 'no chance to repent'), and Israel's failure in Rom.11.7 leads to hardening presented as a settled state ('the rest were hardened'). But other cases show seeking leading to attainment and reversal of separation (Prov.8.17 'find me'; Hos.5.15 leads to God's return). The transformation's reversibility depends entirely on timing and divine response, not on the intensity of the seeking itself.

7171.text: Yes, the mechanism differs sharply by context. In devotional contexts the mechanism is voluntary, inward pursuit toward God/wisdom (Ps.63.1, Prov.8.17, Heb.11.6). In judicial contexts the mechanism is imposed accountability -- an external divine reckoning exacted from a party regardless of their will (Luke.11.50-51, passive 'will be required'). In testing contexts the mechanism is demand made of another as proof/leverage (Matt.16.4, epizeteo demanding a sign). In physical-need contexts the mechanism is survival-driven foraging (Job.24.5).

7172.text: The evidence points to both created design and fallen distortion. The created-design pole appears where seeking God is the proper human posture (Heb.11.6, Ps.63.1, Prov.8.17, Acts.15.17) -- an intended capacity oriented toward God as its fulfillment. The fallen-condition pole appears where seeking is either absent altogether (Rom.3.11, 'no one seeks for God') or twisted into hostile demand (Matt.16.4, testing sign-seeking) or exacted judicially against guilt (Luke.11.50-51). The same capacity for intensive seeking is thus shown as originally God-directed but corruptible into either default neglect or adversarial demand.

7173.text: In devotional occurrences the felt quality is intense and bodily: Ps.63.1 pairs 'earnestly I seek' with 'my soul thirsts... my flesh faints,' and Isa.26.9 pairs it with 'my soul yearns... in the night.' These are not settled dispositions alone but acute, felt longing, expressed through explicit bodily/emotional language (thirst, fainting, yearning at night).

7174.text: In Heb.12.17, the felt quality is transient and grief-laden -- Esau's seeking is marked explicitly by 'tears,' a momentary, desperate emotional response to loss rather than a settled disposition.

7175.text: In the sign-demanding occurrences (epizeteo) no emotion-language accompanies the act itself; instead Mark.8.12 records Jesus's own emotional response to the demand ('he sighed deeply in his spirit'), locating the felt-quality language on the recipient of the demand rather than the demanding party -- record none for the seekers' own inner state here.

7176.text: The felt quality varies sharply by context: acute bodily/emotional intensity in devotional seeking (Ps.63.1, Isa.26.9), grief in failed retrospective seeking (Heb.12.17), settled ongoing disposition in pilgrim-seeking (Heb.11.14, Heb.13.14, presented without emotion-language as a simple ongoing orientation), and no stated inner feeling at all in the judicial/demanding occurrences (Luke.11.50-51, Matt.16.4) where the term functions almost mechanically as legal exaction or test.

7177.text: Yes. The mode varies by direction and context: human-to-God seeking operates inwardly/volitionally (Ps.63.1, Prov.8.17, Heb.11.6); God-to-human/generation operates judicially through passive exaction (Luke.11.50-51, 'will be required'); person-to-person demanding operates confrontationally through speech (Matt.16.4, 'seeks for a sign' addressed to Jesus); person-to-object/need operates through physical activity (Job.24.5, foraging for game). The same lexical family thus spans volitional, judicial, verbal, and physical modes depending on the relational direction.

7178.text: Yes. The sign-demanding occurrences of epizeteo are explicitly communicative -- the generation addresses Jesus directly, demanding he speak/perform a sign (Matt.12.39, Matt.16.4, Mark.8.12, Luke.11.29). Likewise Acts.19.39 shows epizeteo operating through formal spoken/legal request in an assembly. Ekzeteo's Luke.11.50-51 use also has a speech-adjacent judicial register ('charged against,' a verdict pronounced), though it is Jesus's own pronouncement rather than a request. Shachar's occurrences are not communicative acts of demand but inward or physically-enacted seeking, with the exception of implied prayer/address to God (Ps.63.1, Job.8.5, 'plead with the Almighty').

7179.text: The characteristic takes hold rightly under conditions of faith and acknowledged need: Heb.11.6 requires belief that God exists and rewards seekers as the precondition; Hos.5.15 and Ps.78.34 show acknowledgment of guilt and repentance as the inner condition preceding earnest seeking; Job.8.5's conditional ('if you will seek God and plead...for mercy') ties right operation to humility and plea for mercy rather than self-justification.

7180.text: The characteristic is blocked or fruitless under conditions of unbelief (Rom.3.11, 'no one seeks for God' as part of a universal indictment of sinfulness), of prior settled disqualification (Heb.12.17, Esau finds 'no chance to repent' though he sought with tears), of hostile testing rather than genuine inquiry (Matt.12.39/16.4, an 'evil and adulterous generation' demands a sign), and of persistent unresponsiveness to prior calls (Prov.1.28, wisdom's earlier call refused, so later diligent seeking finds no answer). No adversarial-spirit interference is shown in any occurrence; blockage arises from the seeker's own unbelief, prior refusal, or a closed opportunity, not from another spirit's distortion.

7181.text: In Heb.12.17, Esau's inner-being state when the characteristic (seeking) is present but does not take hold is one of grief without genuine repentance -- the text specifies 'he found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears,' showing tears/emotion present but the deeper reorientation of repentance absent, so the seeking remains superficial regret rather than a transformed inner state.

7182.text: Yes. Within existing covenantal bonds (Israel and God), seeking operates as restorative return after distress (Hos.5.15, Ps.78.34) -- an insider's turning back. Across relational distance/difference (Gentiles, outsiders), seeking operates as a fresh, boundary-crossing inclusion: Acts.15.17 explicitly extends ekzeteo to 'the remnant of mankind... and all the Gentiles who are called by my name,' widening the covenantal seeking beyond Israel's existing bond.

7183.text: The characteristic crosses covenantal boundaries: while most OT (shachar) occurrences operate within Israel's covenant relationship with YHWH, Acts.15.17 (ekzeteo, quoting Amos 9:12 LXX) explicitly extends the seeking-of-the-Lord motif to Gentiles 'who are called by my name,' showing the characteristic is not confined to covenant insiders but is projected forward to include outsiders under a widened covenantal frame.

7184.text: The relational scope is universal in principle (Rom.3.11's indictment applies to 'no one' -- all humanity; Acts.15.17 explicitly includes Gentiles) but realized unevenly: the elect obtain what is sought while 'the rest' do not (Rom.11.7), and the sign-demanding generation is characterized as excluded from the category of genuine seekers by its own 'evil and adulterous' disposition (Matt.12.39). Inclusion is thus universal in offer but differentiated in outcome by faith/unbelief.

7186.text: The human-to-God movement of seeking requires an inner posture of humility, acknowledged need, and expectant faith: Job.8.5 pairs seeking God with pleading for mercy; Heb.11.6 requires prior belief in God's existence and rewarding nature; Ps.63.1 and Isa.26.9 show the posture as one of felt lack (thirst, yearning) reaching toward fulfillment; Prov.8.17 frames the posture as love paired with diligence.

7187.text: The human-to-God direction shows a relationship of dependent trust and reward-expectation, not self-sufficiency: the person who seeks believes God exists, rewards seekers (Heb.11.6), and can be found by diligent seekers (Prov.8.17, Jer-style promise pattern) -- the relationship is one where God is approachable and responsive to genuine seeking, contrasted starkly with Rom.3.11's indictment that fallen humanity does not by default seek God at all.

7188.text: Where seeking is rightly directed toward God as its intended fulfillment (D5.2.3/D11.1.1's created-design pole), it instantiates the divine-image aspect of relational orientation toward God -- the capacity to reach, desire, and pursue communion with one's maker, mirroring (in creaturely form) God's own initiative-taking and pursuing character (cf. God's own seeking of Israel, Hos.5.15's 'I will return... until they... seek my face').

7189.text: The characteristic appears shared in analogous form rather than identical: God himself is depicted as one who withdraws until sought (Hos.5.15, 'I will return again to my place, until they... seek my face'), showing a divine parallel to the human act of seeking, though God's 'seeking' or withholding operates from a position of sovereign initiative while the human seeking operates from dependent need -- an analogous but asymmetrical sharing rather than an identical shared capacity.

7190.text: Where the characteristic is present as genuine, faith-grounded pursuit of God (Heb.11.6, Ps.63.1), it indicates the divine image functioning rightly in its relational orientation toward God. Where it is absent entirely (Rom.3.11, universal indictment) it indicates the divine image's relational faculty toward God is disabled/inoperative in fallen humanity apart from grace. Where it is present but distorted into hostile demand (Matt.16.4) it indicates the image's capacity for genuine relational reaching has been turned toward self-justifying testing instead.

7191.text: The evidence engages spirit/soul-level seats primarily (Ps.63.1: 'my soul thirsts'; Isa.26.9: 'my spirit within me earnestly seeks') with body given expressive rather than causal role ('my flesh faints for you' as an outward sign of the soul's longing, not a bodily-originated act). The judicial/demand occurrences (Luke.11.50-51, Matt.16.4) engage no inner-constitutional level explicitly, operating instead at the level of corporate/legal accountability. The body link where present is expressive/indicative -- signaling the intensity of soul-level longing -- never the seat or origin of the seeking itself.

7192.text: In Ps.63.1 the body link runs from soul to body expression: the soul's thirst (inner seeking-longing) is expressed outwardly in the flesh's fainting -- the direction is soul/spirit expressing through the body, not the body generating or feeding back to shape the soul's seeking.

7194.text: God extends the characteristic (or its reward) both conditionally and responsively: Heb.11.6 makes finding God conditional on faith and seeking; Job.8.5 frames restoration as conditional on Job's own seeking and pleading; Hos.5.15 shows God's own withdrawal as conditional and responsive -- he 'returns' precisely when guilt is acknowledged and his face sought, showing the divine response is contingent on the human seeking act rather than unconditional.

7195.text: God's extension of reward/response to seekers shows a disposition of genuine responsiveness and reward-giving rather than aloofness: he 'rewards those who seek him' (Heb.11.6) and promises 'find me' to diligent seekers (Prov.8.17), and his withdrawal in Hos.5.15 is itself framed as purposeful, aimed at provoking the very seeking that will restore relationship -- disciplinary rather than punitive abandonment.

7196.text: In Prov.8.17, personified Wisdom's genuine extension of herself to seekers is accompanied by her own prior orientation of love toward them ('I love those who love me') -- reciprocal affection precedes and accompanies her being found, showing the giver's inner condition is one of settled favor toward the seeker, not indifference.

7197.text: The evidence does not clearly show what a human giver must have received or become before extending this characteristic to another person (as opposed to God extending it) -- the subgroup's occurrences focus on humans seeking God/objects or God/Wisdom being sought, not on one human person extending intensive-seeking to another; this may be resolvable with cross-cluster comparison but is not resolvable from this subgroup's own evidence alone.

7198.text: Uptake of a demand from another is blocked by hostility/unbelief and enabled by right disposition: the evil/adulterous generation's demand for a sign (Matt.16.4) receives refusal from Jesus precisely because the demand itself is untrusting; by contrast the proconsul Sergius Paulus's 'sought to hear the word of God' (Acts.13.7) is accompanied by intelligence/openness and leads to a productive hearing.

7199.text: In Matt.16.4/Matt.12.39/Mark.8.12/Luke.11.29, the generation that demands a sign but is refused one is characterized inwardly as 'evil and adulterous' -- its inner-being state is one of settled unbelief and covenant-unfaithfulness, so the demanding itself is diagnostic of a corrupted heart rather than genuine openness.

7201.text: No occurrence in this subgroup shows the characteristic being communicated, strengthened, or mediated through angelic ministry; all instances of extension or blocking are attributed to God directly, to Christ, to Wisdom personified, or to human agents -- angelic mediation is entirely absent from the evidence.

7202.text: The origin is multiple and changes with context: it originates from divine initiative in judicial contexts (God's demand exacted, Luke.11.50-51), from human volition in devotional contexts (the individual's own choice to seek God, Ps.63.1, Job.8.5), and from collective/corporate disposition in the sign-demanding contexts ('this generation' as a corporate moral agent, Matt.16.4). No single fixed origin holds across all occurrences.

7203.text: The characteristic consistently engages volitional and affective faculties (will/desire: Ps.63.1's thirst, Prov.8.17's love-paired diligence) and occasionally cognitive faculties (belief, Heb.11.6's 'must believe'), but rarely engages purely rational/discursive faculties in isolation -- even the 'searched and inquired carefully' of 1Pet.1.10 (investigative diligence) is paired with prophetic revelation rather than autonomous reasoning. This pattern indicates the characteristic's nature is fundamentally an act of the whole person's directed will and desire toward an object, not a purely intellectual exercise.

7204.text: The characteristic is primarily an ACT -- an enacted operation of intensive seeking or demanding, attested grammatically almost exclusively as verbs (active, passive, participial) across all three member strongs, rather than as a noun-form disposition, condition, or quality. Where it recurs habitually (e.g. Heb.13.14's ongoing pilgrim-seeking, or 'this generation' repeatedly demanding a sign) it functions as a repeated act rather than a distinct static disposition-noun.

7205.text: The characteristic is compound in structure: each member combines a base 'seek' root with an intensifying element -- ekzeteo (ek- 'out/thoroughly' + zeteo), epizeteo (epi- 'upon/toward' + zeteo), and shachar (an inherently intensive root tied etymologically to 'dawn/early,' functioning as a built-in intensifier rather than a compounded prefix). The constituent elements are: (1) the base act of seeking, and (2) an added element of thoroughness, direction, or urgency.

7207.text: The characteristic excludes/resists casual or half-hearted inquiry at its edge -- its intensifying prefixes/root explicitly mark it off from a merely passing glance or occasional interest (zeteo's plain form); it also resists premature closure, refusing to settle for partial or token search (Prov.1.28's failed 'diligent' seeking shows the characteristic still names genuine effort even when unsuccessful, distinguishing it from giving up).

7208.text: The characteristic ends where finding/obtaining begins -- it is not the possession of the object but the reaching toward it (Prov.8.17's 'seek me diligently find me' shows seeking as the antecedent act distinct from finding, the consequent state); it is also distinct from mere calling/asking (a single request) since it implies sustained, thorough effort rather than a single utterance, and distinct from settled belief/perception (M0.1.1's judgement-content) since it is the pursuit that may precede, follow, or accompany belief rather than being identical with it.

7209.text: Adjacent characteristics recur across the subgroup's verses: faith/belief (Heb.11.6, pistis-family), understanding (Rom.3.11, paired negation with G4920), grace/salvation (1Pet.1.10), repentance (Heb.12.17, Hos.5.15, Ps.78.34), love (Prov.8.17, Prov.13.24), guilt-acknowledgment (Hos.5.15), and hardening (Rom.11.7). Faith/belief and repentance are the most frequent co-occurring characteristics, appearing across multiple member strongs.

7210.text: The co-occurrence pattern shows this characteristic sits at a hinge-point in the inner-being landscape: it regularly pairs with cognitive/relational preconditions (faith, belief, guilt-acknowledgment, repentance) that must be present for it to operate rightly, and with outcome-states (finding/reward, or hardening/failure) that follow from whether it is taken up successfully -- marking intensive seeking as a pivotal, transitional characteristic rather than a self-contained end-state.

7211.text: A recurring sequence: acknowledgment of guilt/distress precedes earnest seeking (Hos.5.15: 'until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face'); repentance accompanies or closely follows seeking (Ps.78.34: 'they repented and sought God earnestly'); and seeking precedes finding (Prov.8.17: 'those who seek me diligently find me'). The consistent order is: acknowledgment/distress -> seeking -> repentance/finding.

7212.text: The sequence is developmental and causal rather than merely correlational: acknowledgment of guilt causally opens the way for seeking (Hos.5.15's 'until'), and seeking causally produces finding (Prov.8.17's promise), showing a real chain of cause-and-effect rather than accidental co-occurrence -- though the chain can be broken (Prov.1.28's failed seeking shows the causal chain is conditioned on timing/prior response, not automatic).

7213.text: Yes -- the characteristic produces finding/attainment as its natural fruit by the mechanism of sustained, thorough pursuit meeting a responsive object: 'those who seek me diligently find me' (Prov.8.17); it also produces reward from God as its fruit (Heb.11.6, 'he rewards those who seek him'), by the mechanism of divine responsiveness to genuine faith-grounded pursuit.

7214.text: Yes -- the characteristic is produced by prior acknowledgment of guilt/distress (Hos.5.15) and by repentance (Ps.78.34), and undergirded by faith/belief as its enabling precondition (Heb.11.6).

7215.text: The characteristic functions as a constituent element of 'drawing near to God' (Heb.11.6 frames seeking as part of what one who 'draws near' must do), and repentance can be seen as a constituent element within some instances of this characteristic (Ps.78.34 pairs 'repented and sought' almost synonymously) -- so the relationship runs in both directions depending on the pairing, without a single fixed containment structure.

7216.text: The nearest neighbor is the base root zeteo ('seek') itself, from which both Greek members (ekzeteo, epizeteo) are compounded. What distinguishes this subgroup's members from plain zeteo is the added intensifying/directing element -- thoroughness (ek-), insistence/direction (epi-), or inherent urgency (shachar's dawn-associated root) -- marking a difference of degree/intensity rather than of basic kind from the plain seeking act.

7217.text: The boundary between this subgroup and plain seeking (zeteo) is precisely the presence of an intensifying morphological element -- a prefix (ek-/epi-) or an inherently urgent root (shachar) -- that marks thoroughness, completeness, insistence, or urgency; wherever that marked element is absent, the act belongs to the base seeking family rather than this intensified subgroup.

7218.text: The distinction from the nearest neighbor (plain zeteo) is one of degree, not kind -- the subgroup's members intensify the same basic act of seeking rather than naming a categorically different action; within the subgroup itself, ekzeteo and epizeteo differ from each other by direction (ek- 'out/thoroughly' vs epi- 'upon/toward,' per prior char_reading observations), while shachar differs from both by constitutional mechanism (an inherent root-level intensifier rather than a compounded directional prefix).

7219.text: In Mark.1.36, the search reveals the disciples' belief that Jesus was findable and needed/wanted -- their perception is that his presence mattered and his whereabouts were currently unknown to them, prompting active pursuit rather than passive waiting.

7220.text: With only one occurrence, whether the characteristic consistently precedes or follows a judgement/belief cannot be established from pattern; in this single instance the search follows an implicit belief (that Jesus was worth finding) and precedes the resulting encounter/conclusion, but no cross-verse pattern is available -- resolvable only if additional occurrences existed, which they do not.

7221.text: No orientation toward a future fullness is evidenced; the single occurrence depicts a bounded, completed search act with no forward-looking trajectory of growth or maturation attached to the term itself.

7222.text: Only one occurrence exists, so consistency or variation of the immediate response across verses cannot be determined from this subgroup's evidence.

7223.text: The sustained effect of the disciples' search (what happened once Jesus was found, and how that shaped their ongoing posture) is not contained in Mark.1.36 itself; resolving this requires the following verses (Mark.1.37-38) where Jesus responds and redirects the mission -- flagged for later synergy-stage cross-check.

7224.text: No transformation of the person is depicted by this verb; it names a discrete search act, not a change of state, so reversibility/irreversibility does not apply.

7225.text: With a single occurrence there is no second context against which to compare the mechanism of searching; whether it would differ (e.g. hostile vs. benign contexts) cannot be shown from this subgroup's evidence alone, though the broader lexical range (LSJ) attests both hostile-pursuit and benign-search mechanisms outside the NT.

7226.text: The capacity to search/pursue intensively belongs to created design -- the disciples' search for Jesus reflects ordinary human faculties of concern, attachment, and initiative rather than any distinctively fallen misuse; the subgroup's classification as 'hostile pursuit' rests on the term's wider attested range, not on this NT instance which shows the faculty used well.

7227.text: The search in Mark.1.36 reads as a transient, situational response (urgency to locate Jesus after he withdrew to pray) rather than a settled disposition; no explicit emotion or bodily-feeling language accompanies the verb itself, though the context (early morning, Jesus having withdrawn alone) implies concern or eagerness on the disciples' part.

7228.text: Only one occurrence exists, so consistency or contextual variation of the felt quality cannot be established from this subgroup's evidence.

7229.text: With a single NT occurrence, variation of the mode of operation by context, direction, or constitutional level cannot be demonstrated from this subgroup's evidence, though the term's attested classical range (military pursuit, herding cattle, metaphorical striving) suggests such variation exists in the wider language even if not shown here.

7230.text: No communicative or speech-based mode is evidenced; the search in Mark.1.36 is a physical/locational act (searching for a person's whereabouts), not a commanded, addressed, or spoken operation.

7231.text: The search takes hold rightly under a condition of felt need or attachment -- the disciples act because Jesus' absence (having withdrawn to pray) creates a gap they seek to close, implying valuing his presence/guidance as the inner condition prompting the search.

7232.text: No blocking, distortion, or adversarial interference of the search is shown in this occurrence; the disciples' search proceeds unimpeded to its natural conclusion (finding Jesus, per the following verses).

7233.text: No case is shown of the characteristic present but failing to take hold; the single occurrence presents the search as straightforwardly enacted and effective (leading to Jesus being found), so this question does not apply to the evidence.

7234.text: The search in Mark.1.36 operates within an existing relational bond (disciples seeking their teacher/leader), not across relational distance or hostility -- this contrasts with the hostile-pursuit sense the subgroup label anticipates, where the characteristic would typically operate across enmity or adversarial distance.

7235.text: No covenantal framing attaches to this occurrence; the search is a straightforward interpersonal (disciple-to-teacher) act without covenantal boundary-crossing language.

7236.text: The relational scope in this occurrence includes only the disciples (Simon and companions) as searchers and Jesus as the sought party -- a bounded, known relational circle; the wider hostile-pursuit sense implied by the subgroup label (pursuer vs. hunted enemy) is not instantiated here, since both parties are already in relationship.

7237.text: No D5.1.1 presence/absence audit data is available for this strong within the given evidence; the single occurrence does not speak to the characteristic's place in the divine image.

7238.text: The occurrence is a human-to-human search (disciples seeking Jesus as a person present among them), not a human-to-God movement, so no inner posture toward God specifically is implied by this occurrence alone; insofar as Jesus is understood christologically, the search could imply seeking posture toward God, but the text itself does not frame it that way.

7239.text: The verse depicts a human-to-human search rather than an explicit human-to-God movement; no direct evidence about the person's relationship with God is shown by this occurrence.

7240.text: No aspect of divine likeness is evidenced by this single occurrence; the search is a natural human faculty (attentiveness, initiative, relational attachment) without clear connection drawn in the text to God's own character or the divine image.

7241.text: No basis in the evidence to determine whether this searching capacity is shared with God or a creaturely analogue; the text does not draw that comparison.

7242.text: The presence of the search characteristic in the disciples (Mark.1.36) shows ordinary functioning relational concern, not an indicator of divine-image condition either way; no such indication is evidenced.

7243.text: The single occurrence engages only the level of embodied action/behaviour (searching, a physical/locational act) with no explicit engagement of spirit or inner-soul vocabulary; there is no body link stated (no bodily-feeling term used), so depth and seat cannot be located beyond the observable behavioural level -- the characteristic's inner root (motive, attachment) is implied contextually but not lexically marked.

7244.text: No body link is evidenced in this occurrence (no bodily/feeling term co-occurs with the search verb), so no direction of soul-to-body or body-to-soul feedback can be established; recorded as none.

7245.text: No movement across constitutional levels (spirit/soul/body) or from an external/angelic source is evidenced; the search is depicted as an ordinary self-initiated human act with no such trajectory described.

7246.text: This occurrence does not depict God extending the characteristic to a person; it is a human search directed at Jesus, so the basis question (conditional/unconditional/covenantal/responsive divine extension) does not apply to this evidence.

7247.text: No divine extension of the characteristic is shown in this occurrence; the search is human-initiated and human-directed, so no disposition of God is evidenced by this term here.

7248.text: No giving/extension of the characteristic from one person to another is depicted; the disciples act on their own initiative to find Jesus rather than receiving or transmitting the searching capacity, so no giver-condition data applies.

7249.text: No prior reception or becoming is depicted as a precondition for the disciples' search; the act arises directly from their situation (Jesus' absence) rather than from something transmitted to them first.

7250.text: No scenario of taking up or resisting the characteristic as received from another person is depicted in this occurrence; it is a self-generated search act, not something offered and accepted/blocked.

7251.text: No case of the characteristic being met but not taken up is shown; the disciples fully enact the search, so no inner-being state of non-uptake is evidenced.

7252.text: No adversarial activity is evidenced at or around this characteristic in its sole occurrence; the search is a benign disciple act, showing no site of adversarial interference here, though the term's broader attested range (hostile pursuit) leaves this open in principle outside this subgroup's actual evidence.

7253.text: No angelic ministry mediates or strengthens the characteristic in this occurrence; the search is entirely a human-initiated act with no angelic involvement described.

7254.text: With only one occurrence, whether the origin of the search is single or multiple, and whether it changes with context, cannot be determined from this subgroup's own evidence; in this instance the origin is the disciples themselves (self-originated), but no comparison point exists.

7255.text: The single occurrence engages only the behavioural/action faculty (physically searching) with no explicit engagement of mind, will, or spirit vocabulary; this narrow engagement suggests the term's nature is fundamentally an act-description (a doing) rather than a faculty-rooted disposition-word.

7256.text: Katadiokō names an act -- a discrete, completed action of searching/pursuing (aorist active indicative) -- rather than a standing disposition, condition/status, or abstract quality.

7257.text: The term is structurally compound at the morphological level (kata- intensive prefix + diōkō 'pursue'), combining an intensifying element with a base pursuit-verb; semantically in its sole NT occurrence it functions simply, as a unitary act of searching, without further constituent elements combined within the single usage.

7258.text: The structural opposite of searching/pursuing is abandonment or neglect -- ceasing to look for, giving up on locating, or indifference to the other's whereabouts; this excludes the active, sustained attention that katadiokō names.

7259.text: At its edge, the characteristic excludes passivity and resignation -- it is defined by active, energetic pursuit, so it resists any reading of merely waiting or hoping without effort to locate the sought person.

7260.text: The characteristic ends where mere casual noticing or incidental awareness begins -- katadiokō is not simply seeing or knowing where someone is, but actively tracking and pursuing until found; it is not identical to general seeking (zeteo) which can be passive inquiry, nor to finding (heurisko) which is the completed result.

7261.text: No other M-code characteristic co-occurs with katadiokō in its sole occurrence (Mark.1.36); the verse's other elements are party/connector (T-role) terms, not characteristics.

7262.text: With no co-occurring characteristic evidenced, no conclusion about the inner-being landscape placement can be drawn from co-occurrence data for this strong.

7263.text: No sequence with another characteristic is evidenced in the sole occurrence; recorded as none.

7264.text: No sequence data exists to classify as causal, developmental, or correlational.

7265.text: No production of another characteristic by this one is shown in the evidence; recorded as none.

7266.text: No characteristic is shown producing this one in the evidence; the search arises directly from the disciples' situation, not from another named inner-being characteristic.

7267.text: No constituent relationship with another characteristic is evidenced; katadiokō stands as its own discrete act-word in the sole occurrence.

7268.text: The nearest neighbour is the more general Greek seeking-verb zēteō ('seek'); katadiokō is distinguished from it by its intensified, sustained, tracking-pursuit quality (kata- prefix), whereas zēteō can denote a single act of looking or inquiring without the sense of dogged pursuit.

7269.text: Where zēteō and katadiokō might overlap (both meaning 'to look for'), the precise boundary is intensity and sustained effort: katadiokō implies continuing, energetic tracking until the sought one is found, while zēteō does not necessarily carry that durative, effortful quality.

7270.text: The distinction from the nearest neighbour (zēteō) is one of degree -- katadiokō is an intensified, more effortful form of the same basic seeking action, not a difference of kind, direction, or constitutional level.

7272.text: In Ps.10.4 the wicked's failure to seek God reveals his conclusion 'There is no God' -- the absence of inquiry is itself diagnostic of a settled unbelief; the characteristic here reveals a negative judgement about God's non-existence or irrelevance.

7273.text: In 2Chr.25.15 Amaziah's seeking of the gods of Edom reveals a mistaken belief that defeated foreign gods retain power worth consulting, a judgement the prophet exposes as irrational ('who did not deliver their own people').

7274.text: In Isa.65.1 God's readiness to be sought by those who did not ask reveals his own disposition/perception that he is available and near even to those not yet oriented toward him -- a divine self-disclosure of gracious accessibility rather than a human perception.

7275.text: Across the verses both patterns occur: seeking/inquiring often precedes a resulting belief or outcome (e.g. 2Chr.14.7 'we have sought the Lord... he has given us peace', Ps.34.4 'I sought the Lord, and he answered me'), while elsewhere the failure or presence of seeking follows from an already-settled disposition (Ps.10.4's pride precedes and explains the non-seeking; 2Chr.12.14's evil is explained by not having set the heart to seek). The characteristic functions bidirectionally as both antecedent to and consequence of belief/judgement.

7276.text: Several occurrences orient the seeker toward a future promised fullness -- life (Amos.5.4,6,14 'Seek...and live'), finding/being found (Jer.29.13 'You will seek me and find me'), and restored peace/prosperity (2Chr.14.7) -- showing darash is not only a present act but a movement toward an anticipated covenantal reward not yet possessed.

7277.text: The immediate response to seeking is varied across contexts: it produces answer/deliverance (Ps.34.4), peace (2Chr.14.7), prospering (2Chr.26.5), being found (Jer.29.13), but also, when directed at illegitimate objects, provokes divine anger (2Chr.25.15) or judgment ('come to nothing', Amos.5.5). The response is consistently proportionate to the legitimacy of the object sought, not uniform in kind.

7278.text: Where the immediate response to seeking is a discrete event (an answer, a deliverance, a single oracle), the sustained effect is a settled state of peace, prosperity, or ongoing relationship: 2Chr.14.7 moves from the single act of seeking to years of peace and building; 2Chr.26.5 links sustained seeking ('as long as he sought the Lord') to sustained prospering, showing the sustained effect is durative and conditional on continued seeking rather than a one-time reward.

7279.text: The transformation associated with seeking is shown as reversible: 2Chr.26.5 explicitly makes prospering conditional and ongoing ('as long as he sought the Lord'), implying cessation of seeking removes the blessing; likewise Asa's earlier seeking (2Chr.14.7) does not guarantee later fidelity (2Chr.16.12 records his later failure to seek the Lord in disease), showing the state produced by seeking is not a permanent, irreversible change of condition.

7280.text: The mechanism of seeking differs by context: toward God it operates through prayer/worship and prophetic mediation (1Kgs.22.8, 2Kgs.3.11 -- via a prophet); toward false gods it operates through idolatrous consultation or necromancy (1Sam.28.7, 2Kgs.1.2 -- via mediums); toward legal/moral matters it operates through investigation and testimony-checking (Deut.13.14, 17.4, 19.18 -- via diligent inquiry and witnesses). The underlying mechanism shifts between mediated divine consultation, illicit occult consultation, and forensic investigation.

7281.text: The capacity to inquire/seek belongs to created design -- humanity's original capacity for relationship and dependence on God through consultation (Exod.18.15, Gen.25.22, 1Sam.9.9) -- but its exercise is repeatedly corrupted by the fallen condition, redirected toward false gods, mediums, and necromancers (1Sam.28.7, Deut.18.11, 2Kgs.1.2, Isa.19.3), showing the characteristic itself spans both created design and fallen misdirection depending on its object.

7282.text: In Ps.77.2 seeking the Lord is presented not as a settled disposition but a distressed, effortful response: 'In the day of my trouble I seek the Lord... my hand is stretched out without wearying; my soul refuses to be comforted' -- bodily and emotional language (stretched-out hand, refusing comfort) accompanies the seeking, marking it as an anguished, sustained act arising from crisis.

7283.text: In 2Chr.20.3 Jehoshaphat's seeking arises from fear ('Jehoshaphat was afraid and set his face to seek the Lord') -- a transient emotional trigger (fear) producing a deliberate devotional response (fasting, seeking), showing the felt quality here is urgent and crisis-driven rather than a calm settled habit.
