7284.text: In 1Chr.22.19 and 2Chr.15.12 seeking is framed as a settled, wholehearted disposition ('set your mind and heart to seek', 'seek the Lord... with all their heart and with all their soul') rather than a transient emotional reaction -- the language of heart/soul signals an internalized, durable orientation.

7285.text: The felt quality of seeking varies by context: it is crisis-driven and emotionally anguished in Ps.77.2 and 2Chr.20.3 (trouble, fear), yet presented as a settled, wholehearted covenantal disposition in 1Chr.22.19, 2Chr.15.12, and 2Chr.22.9 ('sought the Lord with all his heart') -- the same term covers both transient emotional response and durable devotional orientation depending on narrative occasion.

7286.text: The mode of operation varies markedly by context: toward God it operates via prayer, worship, and prophetic mediation (1Kgs.22.8, Ps.77.2); toward idols/mediums it operates via necromancy and consultation of the dead (1Sam.28.7, Deut.18.11, Isa.8.19); in judicial contexts it operates via formal investigation and cross-examination of witnesses (Deut.13.14, 17.4, 19.18, Judg.6.29); and toward abstract objects (justice, welfare, a lost object) it operates as diligent practical pursuit (Isa.1.17, Deut.22.2). The constitutional level engaged also varies -- from whole-hearted devotion (soul/heart level) to procedural legal action (behavioral level).

7287.text: Yes, darash regularly operates through speech: it is commanded imperatively ('Inquire first for the word of the Lord', 1Kgs.22.5; 'Seek the Lord and live', Amos.5.4/6/14), addressed as divine self-disclosure ('I will not be inquired of by you', Ezek.20.3), and enacted as spoken request to a prophet or oracle (2Kgs.22.13 'Go, inquire of the Lord for me'). The act of seeking is frequently voiced as command, plea, or reported speech rather than silent internal disposition alone.

7288.text: Seeking takes hold rightly under conditions of wholeheartedness and sincerity: 'set your mind and heart to seek' (1Chr.22.19), 'with all their heart and with all their soul' (2Chr.15.12), and freedom from co-present idolatry -- in Ezek.14.7 the presence of idols in the heart is what disqualifies otherwise-outward consultation. Genuine seeking requires an undivided heart free from rival objects of devotion.

7289.text: Seeking is blocked or nullified when the heart harbors idols or a stumbling block of iniquity even while outwardly consulting God -- Ezek.14.3, 14.7 explicitly describe men who 'have taken their idols into their hearts' yet 'come to a prophet to consult me' -- God declares he will not let himself be consulted (or will answer in judgment) in such cases; similarly pride (Ps.10.4 'in the pride of his face') suppresses seeking altogether.

7291.text: The characteristic operates differently within an existing covenant bond versus across relational distance: within Israel's covenant with God it is commanded and expected as ongoing devotion (2Chr.15.12, Deut.4.29), whereas toward foreign/false deities or across the covenant boundary it is explicitly forbidden and provokes judgment (Deut.12.30 'do not inquire about their gods'; 2Chr.25.20 'sought the gods of Edom'). The same act of seeking is covenant-faithful or covenant-breaking depending entirely on which relational bond it serves.

7292.text: The characteristic clearly crosses covenantal boundaries in the evidence -- it is used both of Israel's covenant-faithful inquiry of the Lord (1Kgs.22.8, 2Chr.15.12) and of pagan/foreign inquiry practices (2Kgs.1.2 inquiring of Baal-zebub; Isa.19.3 Egyptians inquiring of idols and mediums), showing darash is not confined to the covenant community's proper object but names the general human act of formal consultation regardless of which deity or authority is addressed.

7293.text: Relational scope is broad in principle (any nation or person may seek any deity or authority) but narrow in legitimacy: the Lord invites 'a people... their God' (Isa.8.19) and even nations beyond Israel are said to inquire of the root of Jesse (Isa.11.10), showing an eschatological widening of inclusion; yet within Israel's own covenant, failure to seek excludes one from covenant blessing and even life (2Chr.15.13 'whoever would not seek the Lord... should be put to death'), showing exclusion is covenantal-moral rather than ethnic.

7294.text: The characteristic's presence marks a person as rightly oriented toward God in covenant fidelity, and its absence marks corruption or apostasy (Ps.10.4, 1Chr.10.14 'He did not seek guidance from the Lord... the Lord put him to death'); this indicates that the capacity to seek/inquire is part of humanity's created relational orientation toward God, and its exercise or neglect functions as a diagnostic marker of the divine image's proper functioning or its corruption in the person.

7295.text: The human-to-God movement of seeking requires an inner posture of wholehearted devotion and humility: 'sets his heart to seek God' (2Chr.30.19), 'seek him with their whole heart' (Ps.119.2), and freedom from pride (contrast Ps.10.4's proud non-seeker) -- the posture is one of self-abasement and undivided attention directed toward the divine object.

7296.text: The human-to-God direction of seeking reveals a relationship of dependence and covenantal trust: the seeker approaches God as the source of guidance, deliverance, and life (Ps.34.4 'I sought the Lord, and he answered me and delivered me'; Amos.5.4 'Seek me and live'), showing the relationship is characterized by the human party's reliance on God's willingness to respond and God's reciprocal availability to be found (Isa.55.6 'while he may be found').

7299.text: Where seeking is present in a person (2Chr.22.9 'sought the Lord with all his heart'), it indicates the divine image is functioning rightly in relational orientation toward God; where absent (Ps.10.4, 1Chr.10.14), it indicates a corrupted or suppressed image-bearing capacity, evidenced by pride and covenant unfaithfulness leading to death.

7300.text: The evidence shows seeking engages the heart/soul level most deeply and consistently ('with all their heart and with all their soul', 2Chr.15.12; 'set your mind and heart', 1Chr.22.19), with the body's role limited to expressive gesture (Ps.77.2's stretched-out hand) rather than being the seat of the characteristic itself. The pattern indicates seeking's depth and seat is the heart/soul (volitional-affective center), while the body-link (where present) is expressive/indicative of the inner state rather than mediating or generative of it -- darash never engages purely bodily/instinctive levels without heart involvement in these texts.

7301.text: Where a body link exists (Ps.77.2's stretched-out hand accompanying seeking), the direction runs from the inner disposition (soul seeking the Lord) outward through the body as an expressive gesture of persistent appeal -- the hand's stretching is the physical enactment of an inward, unwearied seeking, not a bodily sensation feeding back to generate the seeking itself.

7302.text: The characteristic does not typically move across constitutional levels from within the person, but rather is directed outward from the person (heart/soul) toward an external source (God, a prophet, an oracle, a false deity) -- the movement is fundamentally relational/directional (person-to-authority) rather than internal (spirit-to-soul-to-body); no instance shows another spirit acting upon the person to produce the seeking itself, though the object sought may itself be a spiritual entity (deity, medium, familiar spirit as in 1Sam.28.7).

7303.text: God's extension of the characteristic (his willingness to be sought/found) is shown as both conditional and responsive: conditional on genuine seeking ('If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever', 1Chr.28.9), yet also shown as gracious and unconditioned in Isa.65.1 ('I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me') -- God's self-disclosure as available to be inquired of exceeds strict conditionality, showing both a covenantal-conditional pattern and a gracious-responsive pattern.

7304.text: God's extension of the characteristic -- his readiness to be sought even by those who did not ask (Isa.65.1) and his invitation 'Seek me and live' (Amos.5.4) -- shows a disposition of gracious accessibility and desire for relationship with humanity, contrasted with his refusal to be inquired of by the unrepentant and idolatrous (Ezek.20.3, 20.31), revealing a disposition that is both inviting and holy/discerning.

7308.text: The characteristic is repeatedly shown as a site of adversarial activity: illegitimate seeking is directed toward mediums, necromancers, and familiar spirits (1Sam.28.7, Deut.18.11, Isa.8.19, Isa.19.3) -- these represent occult/adversarial channels that counterfeit legitimate divine consultation, showing darash's object can be corrupted into a vehicle for engaging with adversarial spiritual power rather than God.

7310.text: The origin of the seeking-impulse is multiple and context-dependent: it arises from fear/crisis (2Chr.20.3, sickness in 2Kgs.1.2), from covenantal command (Deut.4.29, 2Chr.15.12), from personal devotion (Ps.119.10 'with my whole heart'), and from national reform initiative (2Chr.34.3, 2Chr.26.5) -- the impulse's source shifts between external threat, internal devotion, and royal/national leadership depending on context, showing no single fixed origin.

7311.text: The pattern of engagement shows heart/soul faculties (mind, will, affection) consistently engaged when seeking is genuine (1Chr.22.19 'set your mind and heart', 2Chr.15.12 'with all their heart and with all their soul'), while purely external/ritual engagement without heart involvement is exposed as illegitimate (Ezek.14.3-7) -- indicating the characteristic's nature is fundamentally a volitional-relational act requiring the engagement of the inner faculties, not a mechanical or merely verbal performance.

7312.text: The characteristic is primarily an ACT (a verb of deliberate consultation/inquiry performed on an occasion), but recurring wholehearted usages ('seek with all your heart', ongoing 'as long as he sought the Lord') show it can also function as a sustained DISPOSITION -- a settled devotional orientation rather than a single event.

7314.text: The structural opposite of seeking is forsaking/neglecting -- explicitly named as the contrastive pole in 1Chr.28.9 ('if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever') and implied by negation in Ps.10.4 ('does not seek') and 1Chr.10.14 ('did not seek guidance') -- the inner-being reality that excludes seeking is self-sufficient neglect or active abandonment of the source that ought to be consulted.

7315.text: At its edge, seeking excludes casual, passive, or half-hearted attention -- it resists mere outward performance without inner devotion (Ezek.14.3-7's idol-hearted consulters are the negative exemplar), and it excludes self-sufficiency/pride that renders inquiry unnecessary (Ps.10.4).

7316.text: Seeking ends and mere physical searching/finding begins where the object sought is a lost item without relational/authoritative dimension (Deut.22.2 'until your brother seeks it' -- retrieving property); it also ends and becomes worship/service where the sustained devotional relationship itself, rather than the discrete act of consultation, is in view (Ezra.6.21 'worship the Lord') -- seeking is thus bounded on one side by mundane recovery and on the other by ongoing cultic devotion.

7317.text: Adjacent characteristics appearing alongside seeking include 'heart/mind' (M47, frequently paired as the seat/manner of seeking, e.g. 1Chr.22.19, 2Chr.15.12, Ps.119.2/10), 'trust' (M19, Ps.9.10, Isa.31.1), and 'forsake' (M30/M59, as antithetical pairing, Ps.9.10, 1Chr.28.9) -- these co-occur with notable frequency, showing seeking is characteristically bound to heart-language and its antithesis, forsaking.

7319.text: Seeking consistently PRECEDES finding/being found and its resulting blessings: Jer.29.13 'You will seek me and find me'; Isa.55.6 'Seek the Lord while he may be found'; 1Chr.28.9 'If you seek him, he will be found by you' -- the sequence is invariably seek-then-find, never the reverse, establishing seeking as the necessary antecedent condition.

7320.text: The seek-then-find sequence is causal-conditional rather than merely correlational or developmental: the finding is explicitly conditioned upon the seeking ('IF you seek him, he WILL be found'), establishing a covenantal cause-and-effect relationship rather than a coincidental temporal succession.

7321.text: Seeking produces peace and prosperity (2Chr.14.7 'we have sought the Lord... he has given us peace on every side'; 2Chr.26.5 'as long as he sought the Lord, God made him prosper') by the mechanism of covenantal blessing responsive to faithful devotion -- the mechanism is relational/covenantal reward rather than mechanical causation.

7322.text: Seeking is itself produced by fear/crisis (2Chr.20.3 'Jehoshaphat was afraid and set his face to seek the Lord') and by covenantal command/exhortation (Deut.4.29, Amos.5.4/6/14 imperatives) -- both an emotional trigger and an external directive can generate the act of seeking.

7323.text: Seeking is a constituent element of the larger characteristic of 'setting the heart' (2Chr.19.3, 2Chr.30.19, 1Chr.22.19 all pair 'set the heart/mind' with 'to seek') -- the heart-setting act supplies the internal disposition of which seeking is the outward-directed enactment, making seeking a component within the fuller act of wholehearted devotion.

7612.text: As already noted: the network is a tight pairing of earnestness qualifying zēteō's seeking-operation; both belong to the same actor and act, with no wider network present.

8097.text: Earnestly serves to intensify Onesiphorus's seeking, marking his search for Paul as diligent rather than casual — it qualifies the manner of his effort, not a separate purpose of its own.

8098.text: The earnestness engages volition — it shows the intensity of Onesiphorus's resolve in seeking Paul out.

8099.text: The earnestness qualifies a human-directed search for Paul, not a movement toward God.

8100.text: This word qualifies Onesiphorus's action toward Paul, not any action of God toward a human.

8101.text: Earnestness is extended by Onesiphorus toward Paul, intensifying the manner of the seeking he directs at him.

8102.text: The verse shows Onesiphorus as the one exercising earnestness, not receiving it from another.

8103.text: No angelic or adversarial being is involved in this human seeking-with-earnestness.

8104.text: Earnestness here is not predicated of God nor related to him; it characterizes Onesiphorus's own effort toward Paul.

8105.text: The immediate effect of this earnestness is the successful finding of Paul, following directly on the intensified search.

8106.text: No lasting inner quality produced in Onesiphorus over time is indicated beyond this single earnest act.

8107.text: No change of state or disposition is depicted; the adverb qualifies manner of an act, not a transformation.

8108.text: No sequence of inner states is shown; the word marks intensity of a single act.

8109.text: No formational mechanism is in view; earnestness here describes manner, not a process producing change.

8110.text: The mode is intensified diligence — earnestness operates as the manner qualifying how vigorously the seeking was carried out.

8111.text: No constitutional level (spirit, soul, heart, mind) is specified for this adverb of manner.

8112.text: The earnestness originates within Onesiphorus himself as his own disposition in seeking Paul out.

9670.text: Seeking here serves Paul: it leads Onesiphorus to be one who does not shrink from finding and helping the imprisoned apostle.

9671.text: The seeking engages volition and relational capacity — Onesiphorus's deliberate will to find and stand by Paul despite his chains.

9672.text: This seeking is directed toward Paul, a fellow believer, not toward God — no movement of worship or supplication to God is shown here.

9673.text: This seeking operates from Onesiphorus toward Paul, not from God toward a human person.

9674.text: Yes: the seeking is extended by Onesiphorus toward Paul, operating as active pursuit until Paul is located and found.

9675.text: The verse shows Onesiphorus as the one extending the seeking, not as a recipient taking it up from another.

9676.text: No angelic or adversarial being is in view; the seeking is a purely human-to-human act.

9677.text: This seeking is not predicated of God nor related to God here; it is Onesiphorus's own act toward Paul.

9678.text: The immediate response shown is successful finding — the seeking issues directly in locating Paul.

9679.text: No lasting inner state in the seeker beyond this single completed act is indicated in the verse.

9680.text: No change of state or disposition in a person is depicted by this seeking; it names an action, not a transformation.

9681.text: No before/during/after sequence of inner states is shown; only the act of seeking and its successful outcome.

9682.text: No mechanism of inner change is in view; this is a reported deed, not a formational process.

9683.text: The mode is active, diligent pursuit — a determined effort to locate a person in a specific place (Rome).

9684.text: No constitutional level (spirit, soul, heart, mind) is specified for this outward action of seeking.

9685.text: The seeking originates within Onesiphorus himself, generated as his own initiative toward Paul.

9686.text: Arrived (ginomai) functions as a plain scene-setting verb marking Onesiphorus's arrival in Rome; it names no distinct inner-being characteristic.

9687.text: The preposition 'in' is a purely locative/grammatical marker with no inner-being characteristic content.

11192.text: Aorist active indicative (searched, 3S) shows a completed, decisive act of seeking Paul out by Onesiphorus, not a vague or ongoing wish.

11193.text: Here the term means an active, diligent hunting-out of a specific person (Paul) in Rome, matching the lexical sense 'to seek/search after' rather than mere desire or inquiry.

11194.text: The searching is directed toward locating Paul personally, implying purposeful effort expended toward another person as its object, culminating in 'found me'.

11195.text: The root sense of active seeking/searching operates here as literal physical searching through Rome to find Paul, not metaphorical seeking.

11196.text: This occurrence matches the term's common sense of physically searching for a person, paralleling e.g. Luke 2:48-49; no divergence from the usual sense.

11197.text: As an aorist active indicative verb, it names a completed act performed by Onesiphorus, presenting the searching as a definite historical event rather than a disposition.

11198.text: Within the term's range from mere desire to intense physical search, this occurrence sits at the concrete 'search after/seek out' end, describing literal effort to locate a person.

11199.text: This occurrence expresses an act (a specific completed search), not a disposition or condition.

11200.text: No structural opposite term for G2212 is present or implied in this verse's context of Onesiphorus searching for Paul.

11201.text: No person-type term (one who habitually seeks) relevant to this occurrence is present in the verse.

11202.text: No supplication/seeking-from-another term relevant to this occurrence appears; the searching here is Onesiphorus seeking Paul directly, not petitioning a third party.

11203.text: As NT Greek narrating a personal historical episode in Rome, Testament context makes no interpretive difference to this occurrence's plain sense of searching.

11204.text: G2212 is well attested in classical Greek (Homer onward) with the same sense of seeking/searching; its use here is not a NT coinage.

11205.text: As an adverb modifying 'searched', its form shows it intensifies the manner of the search rather than naming a standalone quality here.

11206.text: Here it denotes the diligent, earnest manner in which Onesiphorus carried out his search for Paul, matching the sense 'with haste/zeal, earnestly'.

11207.text: The term's implication here is intensifying: it marks the effort behind the search as vigorous and unrelenting, elevating the act of seeking Paul to something costly and deliberate.

11208.text: The root sense tied to haste/zeal operates here to describe the intensity with which the search was conducted, not a leisurely or casual effort.

11209.text: As an adverb, its grammatical form shows it modifies the verb 'searched', qualifying the manner of that action rather than standing as an independent noun/quality.

11210.text: Within the semantic range from literal haste to moral earnestness/zeal, this occurrence sits at the zealous-effort end, describing intensity of a personal search rather than a moral virtue in the abstract.

11211.text: This occurrence expresses an act-qualifying manner (how the search was performed), not a disposition, condition, or received quality of its own.

11212.text: No structural opposite term is present in this verse for the earnest manner of the search.

11213.text: No person-type term (one who habitually acts earnestly) relevant to this occurrence is present in the verse.

11214.text: No supplication/seeking-from-another term relevant to this occurrence is present; the earnestness modifies Onesiphorus's own search, not a plea to another.

11215.text: As NT Greek describing a personal historical act, Testament context makes no interpretive difference to this occurrence's plain adverbial sense.

11216.text: The adverbial form spoudaios/spoudaios-related usage (spoude, 'earnestness/zeal') is attested in classical Greek from the 5th century BC onward; not a NT coinage.

13003.text: The answer it meets: "A soft answer turns away wrath"; "A gift in secret averts anger"; Moses' plea; "when he humbled himself the wrath of the Lord turned from him"; Aaron's reason, "And when Moses heard that, he approved"; Naaman's servants; "His father came out and entreated him"; Jesus called the ten; Gamaliel's counsel. Or none: "I sought for a man … but I found none"; "I looked, but there was no one to help".

13014.text: Who else is in the scene: an intercessor (Exo 32:11); an onlooker whose gladness bears on it (Pro 24:18); a prophet sent with a question (2Ch 25:15); an angel who asks "how long" (Zec 1:12); destroying angels (Psa 78:49); the created world (Jer 7:20); brothers who "exhort one another every day" (Heb 3:13); the authority, "an avenger who carries out God's wrath" (Rom 13:4).

13017.text: What follows a person's anger is where the cases differ (v2, U1 §37): the face falls: "So Cain was very angry, and his face fell"; speech: "I must speak, that I may find relief"; counsel: "I took counsel with myself"; fear: "And David was afraid of the Lord that day"; mercy: "Not a man shall be put to death this day".

13019.text: The leader bears it differently from the people (v2, U2 §65 point 4): Moses: "But the Lord was angry with me because of you"; Aaron "stood between the dead and the living"; David: "let your hand be against me and against my father's house"; and none found: "I sought for a man among them who should build up the wall and stand in the breach before me for the land … but I found none".

13035.text: A person's anger leads to an act at once, with the hand: Moses "threw the tablets out of his hands and broke them"; Balaam "struck the donkey with his staff"; Bigthan and Teresh "sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus".

13053.text: A person responds to God's anger by plead: "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak" (Gen 18:30).

13082.text: The humbling that turned the wrath, and the heart still not set: "And he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the Lord".

13095.text: Sequence in Gen 44:18–45:8: Judah's plea against anger → Joseph weeps → "dismayed" → "do not be … angry with yourselves" → reframing: "not you … but God".

13097.text: Sequence in 1Sa 1:6–18: provoked year by year → weeping, not eating → heart named by husband → "deeply distressed" (Hebrew bitter of soul) → heart-prayer, lips only → misread as drunk → self-explanation ("vexation") → blessing → eats, face no longer sad.

13106.text: Sequence in 2Ch 16:9–12: diagnosis of a failed heart → rage at the seer → cruelty → disease → not seeking the Lord.

13108.text: Sequence in Neh 5:5–9: an outcry heard → anger → "I took counsel with myself" (Hebrew my heart took counsel) → charges → public assembly.

13111.text: Sequence in Job 32:1–20: the friends fall silent → anger ×3 → waiting from deference and fear → "the spirit in man" → belly like wine with no vent → "I must speak, that I may find relief".

13126.text: Sequence in Num 11:1–15, 33: complaint → fire → cry to Moses → prayer → craving → Moses asks to die → plague.

13150.text: Sequence in Eze 22:17–31: dross → melted in the furnace → every rank has failed → "I sought for a man … and stand in the breach … but I found none" → indignation poured out.

13177.text: Anger and Shame (M07): "They shall be ashamed of their harvests because of the fierce anger"; the provocation is "to their own shame"; the incensed "put to shame"; Ezra "ashamed to ask the king".

13197.text: What sets a person's anger off: demand → anger → "Am I in the place of God" (Gen 30:1–2); no regard → very angry → face fell (Gen 4:5); saw no homage → filled with fury → sought to destroy all the Jews (Est 3:5–6); "I thought" → rage (2Ki 5:11–12); afraid → withdraw → enraged (Dan 11:30); heard → filled with wrath → drove him out (Luk 4:28–29); passions at war within → quarrels (Jam 4:1).

13200.text: What does not turn it: godless, folly spoken → anger not turned (Isa 9:17); Manasseh's provocations → did not turn from the burning (2Ki 23:26); sought a man to stand in the breach → found none → poured out my indignation (Eze 22:30–31).

13203.text: What turns or settles a person's anger: soft answer → wrath turned (Pro 15:1); good sense → slow to anger (Pro 19:11); Aaron's answer → Moses heard → approved (Lev 10:16–20); servants' question → dipped → flesh restored (2Ki 5:13–14); poured out her soul, "Go in peace" → ate, face no longer sad (1Sa 1:15–18); sold me → angry with yourselves → do not, for God sent me (Gen 45:5); remember your brother has something against you → first be reconciled (Mat 5:23–24).

13735.text: Whose seat the anger points to, The life or spirit that receives the anger (human, the effect): genuine links Jer 49:37 / 51:45 life; Isa 57:16 "the spirit would grow faint before me"; Job 6:4 "my spirit drinks their poison"; Psa 38:3 flesh. What it implies for the no-seat verses: The laments and penitential psalms: Psa 6:1; 38:1; 88:7, 16 ("your wrath lies heavy upon me"); 90:7, 9 ("by your wrath we are dismayed … we bring our years to an end like a sigh"); Lam 3:1 ("I am the man who has seen affliction under the rod of his wrath"). The receiver's dismay is the inner operation, and the seat is implied from these links.

13802.text: 2Cor 12:20 (5L Anger in the lists of what is put away): Paul fears the quarrel, jealousy and anger he may find.

13887.text: Zep 2:3, "Seek the Lord, all you humble of the land, who do his just commands; seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the Lord": the call comes before "the burning anger of the Lord" (2:2); the people called are already humble and already doing his commands, and are told to seek humility; the verse promises nothing, "perhaps"; being hidden is God's act.

13977.text: Lam 1:11 "revive their strength" (nephesh): appetite/life-sense, not found in the batches.

14034.text: What it leads to. Arrest (Act 4:3), the reframing (above), and in Joh 7:25, the people's question, "Is not this the man whom they seek to kill?". The indignation borders on the plan to kill. Compare Mar 3:6 (§32).

14046.text: Every request is granted, and no anger comes. "I will not do it, if I find thirty there" (Gen 18:30); "God did so that night" (Judg 6:40). The anger feared never appears in either passage.

14093.text: Seeking favour: "Jehoahaz sought the favor of the Lord, and the Lord listened to him, for he saw the oppression of Israel" (2Ki 13:4).

14102.text: Humbling that is partial. Rehoboam is spared destruction but made to serve Shishak, "that they may know my service and the service of the kingdoms" (2Ch 12:8). Bronze shields replace gold (12:10). And "he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the Lord" (12:14). The humbling turned the wrath, and the heart was still not set.

14106.text: 2Ch 12:14 "did not set his heart to seek the Lord".

14191.text: (c) Rebuked by a holy person: Asa, told by the seer that he "relied on the king of Syria", "was angry with the seer and put him in the stocks … for he was in a rage with him" (2Ch 16:10). The rage spreads: "Asa inflicted cruelties upon some of the people at the same time" (16:10); Uzziah, withstood by the priests at the altar: "Uzziah was angry … and when he became angry with the priests, leprosy broke out on his forehead" (2Ch 26:19); In both, the anger is against the messenger of a boundary, and the story ends with the angry king's own body struck: Asa "diseased in his feet … Yet even in his disease he did not seek the Lord" (16:12); Uzziah "a leper to the day of his death" (26:21).

14199.text: What it does to those beneath it: Pleading against it before it rises:; Judah: "let not your anger burn against your servant, for you are like Pharaoh himself" (Gen 44:18). The plea is a long retelling of the father's love (44:19–21 onward); Rachel: "Let not my lord be angry that I cannot rise before you, for the way of women is upon me" (Gen 31:35). The plea for no anger covers a concealment: she is sitting on the stolen gods (31:34); Reading it as a sign: "If he says, 'Good!' it will be well with your servant, but if he is angry, then know that harm is determined by him" (1Sa 20:7). Saul's anger is to be read as the evidence of Saul's intent. Jonathan's knowledge follows the same path: after the spear, "Jonathan knew that his father was determined to put David to death" (20:33); Anticipating it and scripting a reply: Joab to the messenger: "if the king's anger rises, and if he says to you, 'Why did you go so near the city?' … then you shall say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also'" (2Sa 11:20–21). The anger is foreseen, and so is the one sentence that will turn it. That sentence works because the king had wanted Uriah dead. The line manages the king's anger by exposing the king's own secret; Plotting against it from below: "Bigthan and Teresh … became angry and sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus" (Est 2:21). This is anger rising from the servants, discovered through Mordecai (2:22); Anger acting covertly: Zebul, "when [he] heard the words of Gaal … his anger was kindled. And he sent messengers to Abimelech secretly" (Judg 9:30–31). Anger turned into an ambush plan, "set an ambush in the field" (9:32); A group overrules its king: "the commanders of the Philistines were angry with him … 'Send the man back … how could this fellow reconcile himself to his lord?'" (1Sa 29:4). The king Achish yields: "Nevertheless, the lords do not approve of you" (29:6). The anger comes from suspicion: they fear a loyalty they cannot see.

14208.text: How it co-exists: With enforced silence first. "Elihu had waited to speak to Job because they were older than he" (32:4), and "I was timid and afraid to declare my opinion" (32:6). Fear and deference hold the anger in, until the others fall silent; Elihu describes the pressure in bodily terms: "I am full of words; the spirit within me constrains me. Behold, my belly is like wine that has no vent; like new wineskins ready to burst. I must speak, that I may find relief" (32:18–20). The held anger is felt as pressure in the belly, and speech is its release.

14215.text: What it leads to: Public action: Nehemiah's "great assembly" and charge (Neh 5:7–9); Vengeance with deceit: the brothers "answered Shechem … deceitfully" (Gen 34:13), and "Simeon and Levi … took their swords and came against the city while it felt secure and killed all the males" (34:25). This is the deed Jacob's curse names in §10; Self-conviction: David; Nothing: David at 13:21; Fasting: Jonathan.

14222.text: What it leads to: Resolution through a word given: Eli's "Go in peace", and then "the woman went her way and ate, and her face was no longer sad" (1Sa 1:17–18). The body's signs reverse: she eats, and her face changes; Or a plea to be allowed to die: "that it would please God to crush me, that he would let loose his hand and cut me off!" (Job 6:9); Or interpretation: Joseph's "Please tell them to me" (Gen 40:8).

14224.text: Part 2 verses: what they add. Three new strands: (a) The eye wasting, as in Job 17:7; "My eye wastes away because of grief; it grows weak because of all my foes" (Psa 6:7), after "every night I flood my bed with tears" (6:6); "My eye is wasted from grief; my soul and my body also. For my life is spent with sorrow" (Psa 31:9–10); The eye is where ka'as shows in the body, in all three texts (Job 17:7; Psa 6:7; 31:9); What turns Psa 6 round is being heard: "the Lord has heard the sound of my weeping. The Lord has heard my plea" (6:8–9). In Psa 10:14, "you do see, for you note mischief and vexation, that you may take it into your hands; to you the helpless commits himself". The vexation is seen by God, and the helpless hands it over; (b) Provocation from those closest; "A foolish son is a grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him" (Pro 17:25); The reverse direction: "Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger" (Eph 6:4), and "do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged" (Col 3:21); Vexation passes both ways between parent and child. Col 3:21 names its outcome as losing heart. Hannah's rival (1Sa 1:6) was a co-wife. These are the family members; (c) Qoheleth's vexation: the vexation of the thinker and the worker; Knowing brings it: "in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow" (Ecc 1:18). This comes after "I applied my heart to know wisdom … this also is but a striving after wind" (1:17); Work brings it, and it keeps the heart awake: "his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest" (2:23); "all his days he eats in darkness in much vexation and sickness and anger" (5:17); Its answer is enjoyment received as God's gift: "There is nothing better … than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God" (2:24), and "this is the gift of God" (5:19); It is to be removed: "Remove vexation from your heart, and put away pain from your body" (11:10), after "Rejoice, O young man … let your heart cheer you" (11:9); It is sometimes better than laughter: "Sorrow [ka'as] is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (7:3). The one place where ka'as is valued. The face is sad and the heart made good. Face and heart go in opposite directions.

14248.text: What it leads to: Withdrawal from what God struck: David will not take the ark home (2Sa 6:10). The anger ends in avoidance, and the ark's blessing goes to Obed-edom instead (6:11); A burden shared: Moses; Obedience with grief: Samuel goes to meet Saul the next morning (15:12).

14269.text: Part 2 verses: what they add (both were B8: human vexation induced by God): Paul reads Deu 32:21 as a statement about understanding: "But I ask, did Israel not understand? First Moses says, 'I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation; with a foolish nation I will make you angry'" (Rom 10:19). Then "I have been found by those who did not seek me" (10:20), and "All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people" (10:21); The induced anger is set inside God's outstretched hands. It is a provocation meant to bring them back, not only a punishment; Compare Deu 32:29, "If they were wise, they would understand this"; God troubles the nations' hearts at another's fall: "I will trouble [ka'as] the hearts of many peoples, when I bring your destruction among the nations" (Eze 32:9), and "They shall tremble every moment, every one for his own life" (32:10). The vexation God induces comes from seeing a great power fall. It is a trouble of the onlooker, and it turns to fear for one's own life.

14271.text: What it does: It reads the rival's heart as evil: Eliab, "I know your presumption and the evil of your heart, for you have come down to see the battle" (1Sa 17:28); It reckons the rival's future: Saul, "They have ascribed to David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed thousands, and what more can he have but the kingdom?" (18:8); It attacks one's own son as the rival's ally: "You son of a perverse, rebellious woman … as long as the son of Jesse lives … neither you nor your kingdom shall be established" (20:30–31); It jeers: Sanballat "was angry and greatly enraged, and he jeered at the Jews … 'What are these feeble Jews doing?'" (Neh 4:1–2); It enlarges its target: Haman "disdained to lay hands on Mordecai alone … sought to destroy all the Jews" (Est 3:6).

14274.text: What it leads to: The spear, twice (1Sa 18:11; 20:33); A plan of genocide (Est 3:6–8); Armed plotting (Neh 4:8); On the other side, prayer and a guard (Neh 4:9), and building on regardless: "the people had a mind to work" (4:6).

14307.text: What it does. It stands among its companions: "envy, murder, strife, deceit" (Rom 1:29); "quarreling and jealousy" (Rom 13:13); "quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder" (2Cor 12:20); "enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy" (Gal 5:20–21); "bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander … malice" (Eph 4:31); "anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth" (Col 3:8).

14314.text: What it leads to. Arrest (Act 4:3), the reframing (above), and in Joh 7:25, the people's question, "Is not this the man whom they seek to kill?". The indignation borders on the plan to kill. Compare Mar 3:6.

14337.text: How it co-exists. In Luk 14:21 anger turns into a wider invitation, not punishment. The anger that invitations were refused fills the house with the poor: "compel people to come in, that my house may be filled" (14:23). Of the three parable angers, one ends in grace to outsiders. Mat 22:8–9 does the same after the destruction: "invite to the wedding feast as many as you find".

14356.text: Part 2 (11): Pro 6:16; 21:23; 22:25; Ecc 2:22; 2:24; Eze 3:12; 1Cor 3:1; 2Cor 7:3; 7:13; 12:18; Rev 3:13. Eze 3:12 and Rev 3:13 are the divine Spirit.

14372.text: Gen 44:18–45:8: Sequence the text gives: Judah's plea against anger → Joseph weeps → "dismayed" → "do not be … angry with yourselves" → reframing: "not you … but God".

14374.text: 1Sa 1:6–18: Sequence the text gives: provoked year by year → weeping, not eating → heart named by husband → "deeply distressed" (Hebrew bitter of soul) → heart-prayer, lips only → misread as drunk → self-explanation ("vexation") → blessing → eats, face no longer sad.

14383.text: 2Ch 16:9–12: Sequence the text gives: diagnosis of a failed heart → rage at the seer → cruelty → disease → not seeking the Lord.

14385.text: Neh 5:5–9: Sequence the text gives: an outcry heard → anger → "I took counsel with myself" (Hebrew my heart took counsel) → charges → public assembly.

14388.text: Job 32:1–20: Sequence the text gives: the friends fall silent → anger ×3 → waiting from deference and fear → "the spirit in man" → belly like wine with no vent → "I must speak, that I may find relief".

14492.text: What it does: Abraham: "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak. Suppose thirty are found there" (Gen 18:30), and at the last: "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak again but this once. Suppose ten" (18:32); Gideon, after the fleece was wet: "Let not your anger burn against me; let me speak just once more. Please let me test just once more with the fleece" (Judg 6:39); The same form appears in two different kinds of asking. Abraham asks for a city he does not belong to. Gideon asks for assurance for himself.

14493.text: How it co-exists: Boldness and restraint in one sentence. The plea not to anger does not stop the asking. It is what allows the asking; Every request is granted, and no anger comes. "I will not do it, if I find thirty there" (Gen 18:30); "God did so that night" (Judg 6:40). The anger feared never appears in either passage.

14515.text: Part B: Psa 86:15; 103:8; 145:8. Three more uses of the name. Pilot §2.2 already lists all three as uses of the idiom: An individual's plea against "insolent men": "But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger … Turn to me and be gracious to me" (Psa 86:14–16); A recital with its reasoning: "He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever. He does not deal with us according to our sins" (103:9–10). This comes straight after "He made known his ways to Moses" (103:7). The psalm names Moses as the one to whom the name was made known; Praise: "The Lord is good to all, and his mercy is over all that he has made" (145:9); The one creed is now used five ways: worship (Exo 34:8), plea (Num 14; Psa 86), confession (Neh 9), complaint and praise (Psa 145); Seat . Outside: Psa 86:13 "you have delivered my soul from the depths of Sheol". The pleader's own. Genuine.

14530.text: How it co-exists: The provocation is inherited. "you have risen in your fathers' place, a brood of sinful men, to increase still more the fierce anger of the Lord" (Num 32:14). The sons are warned that they are repeating the fathers. They answer by offering to go armed before their brothers (32:16–17); Remembering is commanded against self-righteousness. "Do not say in your heart … 'It is because of my righteousness'" (Deu 9:4); "Remember and do not forget how you provoked the Lord your God to wrath in the wilderness" (9:7). Memory of provoking God is the cure for the heart's claim to righteousness; Moses caught between. In Num 11:10–15 Moses hears the weeping, is "displeased", and says: "Why have you dealt ill with your servant? … kill me at once … that I may not see my wretchedness" (11:11, 15). The leader between God's anger and the people's complaint asks to die.

14536.text: Where it comes from: From rivalry (Miriam and Aaron, Num 12:1–2, not read here); From loss of the restraining figure: "after the death of Jehoiada the princes … paid homage to the king. Then the king listened to them" (2Ch 24:17); From pride after victory: Amaziah worships "the gods of a people who did not deliver their own people from your hand" (2Ch 25:15).

14563.text: What it does: Given over: "he gave them over to plunderers … so that they could no longer withstand their enemies … And they were in terrible distress" (Judg 2:14–15); Crying out: "when the people of Israel cried out to the Lord, the Lord raised up a deliverer" (Judg 3:9); "We have sinned against you, because we have forsaken our God" (10:10); "do to us whatever seems good to you. Only please deliver us this day" (10:15); Seeking favour: "Jehoahaz sought the favor of the Lord, and the Lord listened to him, for he saw the oppression of Israel" (2Ki 13:4); Relapsing: "whenever the judge died, they turned back and were more corrupt than their fathers … They did not drop any of their practices or their stubborn ways" (Judg 2:19); "Nevertheless, they did not depart from the sins of the house of Jeroboam" (2Ki 13:6).

14576.text: How it co-exists: Humbling with a confession of God's justice: "The Lord is righteous" (2Ch 12:6); "you are just" (Ezr 9:15); Humbling with the body: torn clothes and weeping (Josiah); Humbling that is partial. Rehoboam is spared destruction but made to serve Shishak, "that they may know my service and the service of the kingdoms" (2Ch 12:8). Bronze shields replace gold (12:10). And "he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the Lord" (12:14). The humbling turned the wrath, and the heart was still not set.

14578.text: Seat: In the verse: 2Ch 32:25 "his heart was proud" and 32:26 "the pride of his heart". Hezekiah's own. Genuine. A v3 §2.2; D v2 §9.1, §10.1, §11; pilot §2; Outside (all genuine, the bearer's own):; 1Ki 8:47–48 / 2Ch 6:37–38 "turn their heart … with all their heart and with all their soul"; 2Ki 22:19 / 2Ch 34:27 "your heart was penitent / tender"; 2Ch 12:14 "did not set his heart to seek the Lord"; Nothing new in any single seat. What part A adds is a third kind of seat for pilot §2. The pilot has the heart that provokes (the cause) and the spirit that receives (the effect). Part A adds the heart that turns, and so turns the anger away. In these verses, and in §22, it is the human seat most often named in the context of God's anger. For the researcher: whether pilot §2 takes this as a third row.

14588.text: Part B: Jer 21:5; 52:3: Jer 52:3 is 2Ki 24:20; "Behold, I will turn back the weapons of war that are in your hands … I myself will fight against you with outstretched hand and strong arm, in anger and in fury and in great wrath" (Jer 21:4–5); "He shall not pity them or spare them" (21:7). God's anger turns the people's own weapons back on them.

14589.text: What it does: Removal: Josiah "removed all the shrines … which kings of Israel had made, provoking the Lord to anger" (2Ki 23:19); Covenant formed in the heart: "Now it is in my heart to make a covenant with the Lord … in order that his fierce anger may turn away from us. My sons, do not now be negligent" (2Ch 29:10–11); A call to return: "Do not now be stiff-necked as your fathers were, but yield yourselves to the Lord … that his fierce anger may turn away from you. For if you return … your brothers and your children will find compassion" (2Ch 30:8–9); Separation: "Let our officials stand for the whole assembly … until the fierce wrath of our God over this matter is turned away from us" (Ezr 10:14); Sabbath restored: "Now you are bringing more wrath on Israel by profaning the Sabbath" (Neh 13:18), then the gates are shut (13:19); Captives released:; Oded: "you have killed them in a rage that has reached up to heaven … Have you not sins of your own against the Lord your God? … send back the captives … for the fierce wrath of the Lord is upon you" (2Ch 28:9–11); The chiefs: "you propose to bring upon us guilt against the Lord in addition to our present sins … there is fierce wrath against Israel" (28:13); Then: "with the spoil they clothed all who were naked among them … provided them with food and drink, and anointed them, and carrying all the feeble among them on donkeys, they brought them to their kinsfolk" (28:15). Fear of adding to the wrath turns into care for enemies who are also kin; Rebuke acted on: "Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the Lord? Because of this, wrath has gone out against you … Nevertheless, some good is found in you … you … have set your heart to seek God" (2Ch 19:2–3). Jehoshaphat "went out again among the people … and brought them back to the Lord" (19:4).

14593.text: Seat: In the verse: 2Ch 29:10 "it is in my heart to make a covenant". Hezekiah's own. Genuine. A v3 §2.2; E v2 §7.1; Outside: 2Ch 19:3 "set your heart to seek God"; The seat of reform is where the intent to turn is formed. This joins §19 (see there).

14594.text: What it does. "For I was ashamed to ask the king for a band of soldiers … since we had told the king, 'The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him, and the power of his wrath is against all who forsake him'" (Ezr 8:22).

14595.text: How it co-exists. Fasting and humbling: "I proclaimed a fast … that we might humble ourselves before our God, to seek from him a safe journey" (8:21). "we fasted and implored our God for this, and he listened" (8:23).

14610.text: How it co-exists: Isolation. "He has put my brothers far from me … My relatives have failed me, my close friends have forgotten me" (19:13–14). "Men have gaped at me with their mouth" (16:10); Not being able to see God. "Behold, he passes by me, and I see him not" (9:11). "If I summoned him and he answered me, I would not believe that he was listening to my voice" (9:16); A wish not to have been born. "Why did you bring me out from the womb?" (10:18). "leave me alone, that I may find a little cheer" (10:20); Hope beyond the anger, in the same breath. "Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past, that you would appoint me a set time, and remember me! … You would call, and I would answer you; you would long for the work of your hands" (14:13, 15). Job asks for a hiding place from God's anger in God's own keeping, and expects God to long for him afterwards.

14618.text: Where it comes from: Sin is named in Psalm 38: "there is no health in my bones because of my sin. For my iniquities have gone over my head … My wounds stink and fester because of my foolishness" (38:3–5). Psalm 6 names no sin; Human limits, in Jeremiah: "I know, O Lord, that the way of man is not in himself, that it is not in man who walks to direct his steps" (10:23).

14623.text: Where it comes from. In Psalm 27, from a seeker who has already answered God's call: "You have said, 'Seek my face.' My heart says to you, 'Your face, Lord, do I seek'" (27:8). The fear of rejection comes after the heart's own seeking.

14626.text: Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Psa 27:8 "My heart says to you". The seeker's own. Genuine.

14670.text: What it does: "Behold, the day of the Lord comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger" (Isa 13:9); "the Lord is enraged against all the nations" (34:2); "the peaceful folds are devastated because of the fierce anger of the Lord" (Jer 25:37); The human side:; "Therefore all hands will be feeble, and every human heart will melt. They will be dismayed: pangs and agony will seize them … They will look aghast at one another; their faces will be aflame" (Isa 13:7–8); "like a hunted gazelle, or like sheep with none to gather them, each will turn to his own people, and each will flee to his own land" (13:14); "No refuge will remain for the shepherds … the cry of the shepherds, and the wail of the lords of the flock!" (Jer 25:35–36); "I will terrify Elam before their enemies and before those who seek their life" (49:37); Onlookers: "everyone who passes by Babylon shall be appalled, and hiss because of all her wounds" (50:13).

14673.text: Seat: In the verse: Jer 49:37 "life". Elam's. Life-sense; Outside: Isa 13:7 "every human heart will melt". Genuine. Not found in the batches: new as a context seat.

14680.text: Part C: Zep 2:2; 2:3; Rev 6:16: Hiding offered, with "perhaps": "Gather together, yes, gather, O shameless nation, before the decree takes effect … Seek the Lord, all you humble of the land … seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the Lord" (Zep 2:1–3). The way to be hidden is seeking, humility and righteousness, and even then only "perhaps"; Hiding from God, not in him: "the kings of the earth and the great ones … and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains, calling to the mountains and rocks, 'Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb'" (Rev 6:15–16); This is the reverse of Isa 26:20. There God calls his people into their chambers. Here people ask the mountains to hide them from God.

14692.text: Part C: Eze 14:19; 22:24; 22:31: "I found none": "And I sought for a man among them who should build up the wall and stand in the breach before me for the land, that I should not destroy it, but I found none. Therefore I have poured out my indignation upon them" (Eze 22:30–31, context read); Ezekiel uses the image of Psa 106:23, to say that no one did; Before it, every group is named as having failed: prophets (22:25, 28), priests (22:26), princes (22:27), the people of the land (22:29); Even the righteous could not stand for others: "even if Noah, Daniel, and Job were in it … they would deliver neither son nor daughter. They would deliver but their own lives by their righteousness" (14:20); Part A §4 had intercession that succeeded. Part C has intercession sought and not found (22:30), refused (9:8–10), and declared insufficient (14:20); Seat . Outside: Eze 14:20 "their own lives" (nephesh). Life-sense. Eze 22:25 "devoured human lives".

14693.text: What it does: "you say, 'I am innocent; surely his anger has turned from me.' Behold, I will bring you to judgment for saying, 'I have not sinned'" (Jer 2:35). This is said to a people with "the lifeblood of the guiltless poor" on their skirts (2:34); The prophets "say continually to those who despise the word of the Lord, 'It shall be well with you'; and to everyone who stubbornly follows his own heart, they say, 'No disaster shall come upon you'" (23:17). The answer: "Behold, the storm of the Lord! Wrath has gone forth" (23:19).

14728.text: Seat: In the verse: none; Outside:; Lam 2:19 "pour out your heart like water"; 3:20 "My soul … is bowed down"; 3:41 "lift up our hearts"; 3:33 "from his heart": God's, divine; Lam 1:11 "revive their strength" (nephesh): appetite/life-sense, not found in the batches.

14769.text: Linked to earlier sections: Part B §43 had "It may be" (Jer 36:7). Part C §39 has "perhaps you may be hidden" (Zep 2:3); Returning that knows no guarantee is a recurring form; Revisit of U1 §13. Jonah's anger at God's mercy (Jon 4) follows this relenting. The mercy he resented was given to a people who turned without knowing it would come.

14979.text: What the passage carries: the men of Israel "withdrew", and Eleazar "rose and struck down the Philistines until his hand was weary, and his hand clung to the sword. And the Lord brought about a great victory that day" (23:10).

14987.text: What the passage adds: "They were silent and could not find a word to say" (5:8), and then, "We will restore these and require nothing from them" (5:12).

15022.text: The passage. A prayer of David from deep water (69:1–2), weary with crying and waiting (69:3), hated "without cause" (69:4), and confessing "you know my folly" (69:5). The middle (69:6–12) is about reproach; the plea follows (69:13–18); then reproach again (69:19–21); and the psalm ends in praise and in "the Lord hears the needy" (69:33).

15024.text: his concern is for others who hope in God: "Let not those who hope in you be put to shame through me" (69:6).

15035.text: The psalm also asks that others not be put to shame "through me" (69:6). I read the one who prays as fearing that his reproach will spread to those who hope in God. The verse states the request; the fear is my reading.

15065.text: The stacked pairs are the paired cries of the psalms and prophets, "let them be put to shame and confounded" (for example Psa 35:4, 26; 40:14; 70:2). H2781 with H7045 is the prophetic list "a reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse" (for example Jer 24:9; 42:18; 44:8, 12).

15087.text: These verses join pride to the turning away from God: Pride is a witness against its owner. "The pride of Israel testifies to his face; yet they do not return to the Lord their God, nor seek him, for all this" (Hos 7:10; also Hos 5:5); It goes with not knowing. The verse before says "Strangers devour his strength, and he knows it not; gray hairs are sprinkled upon him, and he knows it not" (Hos 7:9). In Hos 5:4–5, "they know not the Lord" stands next to "The pride of Israel testifies to his face"; Pride does not listen; "Hear and give ear; be not proud, for the Lord has spoken" (Jer 13:15). The opposite of pride here is hearing; Then: "if you will not listen, my soul will weep in secret for your pride" (13:17); The pride God will "spoil" belongs to a people "who refuse to hear my words, who stubbornly follow their own heart" (13:9–10); Pride leaves a cry unanswered; "There they cry out, but he does not answer, because of the pride of evil men" (Job 35:12); The cry has no turning to God in it: "none says, 'Where is God my Maker'" (35:10); I read: this cry is a cry of pain that does not seek God; God works to keep pride from a man. He speaks "in a dream ... that he may turn man aside from his deed and conceal pride from a man; he keeps back his soul from the pit" (Job 33:15–18). God's warning is aimed at pride before it ripens; The wicked does not see. "If favor is shown to the wicked, he does not learn righteousness ... and does not see the majesty of the Lord" (Isa 26:10). Not seeing God's majesty sits in the same verse as not learning from his favour.

15117.text: It has no room for God: "In the pride of his face the wicked does not seek him; all his thoughts are, 'There is no God'" (Psa 10:4); "his soul is puffed up; it is not upright within him, but the righteous shall live by his faith" (Hab 2:4). Then: "an arrogant man who is never at rest. His greed is as wide as Sheol" (2:5). The swollen soul is set against faith, and joined to restlessness and greed.

15118.text: It is seen in the eyes, the walk and the house: "Haughty eyes and a proud heart, the lamp of the wicked, are sin" (Pro 21:4). It follows "the Lord weighs the heart" (21:2); "Whoever has a haughty look and an arrogant heart I will not endure" (Psa 101:5); The daughters of Zion "walk with outstretched necks, glancing wantonly with their eyes" (Isa 3:16), in the same oracle as "the spoil of the poor is in your houses" (3:14); "he who makes his door high seeks destruction" (Pro 17:19); "How sick is your heart ... the deeds of a brazen prostitute" (Eze 16:30).

15123.text: Rising up, with God not set before them. "insolent men have risen up against me; a band of ruthless men seeks my life, and they do not set you before them" (Psa 86:14). The answer is "But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious" (86:15).

15138.text: A heart lifted up in the ways of the Lord. Jehoshaphat "sought the God of his father and walked in his commandments ... His heart was courageous in the ways of the Lord" (2Ch 17:4–6). The word is gābah, the one used for Uzziah's and Hezekiah's proud hearts: I read: the lifting is the same; the direction differs. Jehoshaphat's heart rose in God's ways and against the high places, not above God; This is a change of character (#1919).

15146.text: The verses say outright that pride takes a place that is God's: "you have said, 'I am a god, I sit in the seat of the gods' ... yet you are but a man, and no god, though you make your heart like the heart of a god" (Eze 28:2); "Who will bring me down to the ground?" (Obd 3); "By the strength of my hand I have done it" (Isa 10:13); This is the researcher's "assumed position" in the verses' own words. Pride is a heart made like the heart of a god. It is not so; What was given is turned into pride; "the Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar ... kingship and greatness and glory and majesty ... But when his heart was lifted up" (Dan 5:18–20). Majesty is the same word family God wears (batch 1); The pattern recurs: Uzziah's strength (2Ch 26:15–16), Hezekiah's healing (2Ch 32:24–25), the cherub's beauty (Eze 28:17), the cedar's height (Eze 31:9–10); I read: the human standing in these verses is real, and it is given. Pride begins when the heart treats it as its own. Batch 1 showed the same in Eze 7:20 and 24:21; God's height does not keep him from the low. "though the Lord is high, he regards the lowly, but the haughty he knows from afar" (Psa 138:6). The high God comes near the lowly. The proud, who make themselves high, are known "from afar"; Lifting up belongs to God. "not from the east or from the west ... comes lifting up, but it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another" (Psa 75:6–7). The one who has height by nature is the one who gives height; God is known as greater through his answer to arrogance. "Now I know that the Lord is greater than all gods, because ... they dealt arrogantly" (Exo 18:11). "you knew that they acted arrogantly ... And you made a name for yourself" (Neh 9:10); God knows and weighs. "Talk no more so very proudly ... for the Lord is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed" (1Sa 2:3). This is joined to "the Lord weighs the heart" (Pro 21:2) beside "a proud heart" (21:4). I read: pride claims a height that cannot bear being weighed. God's knowing is part of what it runs into; His mercy answers presumption. "they acted presumptuously ... But you are a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful" (Neh 9:16–17). "insolent men have risen up against me ... But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious" (Psa 86:14–15).

15151.text: The Greek picture is swelling, physioō, "to inflate". In Paul it is set again and again against love: Knowledge. "This 'knowledge' puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know. But if anyone loves God, he is known by God" (1Co 8:1–3). Swelling knowledge is answered not by more knowledge but by being known by God; Love is not. "Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant" (1Co 13:4). Before this: "if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge ... but have not love, I am nothing" (13:2); Party; "that none of you may be puffed up in favor of one against another. For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1Co 4:6–7); Here Paul states what the Hebrew verses showed in story: pride holds what was received "as if you did not receive it"; Talk without power. "Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you ... I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power. For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power" (1Co 4:18–20). The arrogance rests on Paul being absent; Where grief belongs. "And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn?" (1Co 5:2). Pride stands where mourning should be; Without reason. "puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind, and not holding fast to the Head" (Col 2:18–19, carried from M09); The new convert. "He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil" (1Ti 3:6). The verse joins conceit to the devil's condemnation. It does not say what the devil's condemnation was. I read: it is held for 13.3 (other spirits). It is not built on here; Controversy. "he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension" (1Ti 6:4). Conceit is joined to understanding nothing, and to quarrels; With pleasure. "swollen with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power" (2Ti 3:4–5); Among the others; "quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder" (2Co 12:20); "Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another" (Gal 5:26), after "let us also keep in step with the Spirit" (5:25); Conceit is named among the things that set people against each other.

15173.text: Conceit among the things that divide people (Gal 5:26; 2Co 12:20; 1Ti 6:4) bears on 10.10, and on 10.6 (envy).

15195.text: The boast is not removed. It is moved: The command. "Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord" (1Co 1:31; 2Co 10:17). This follows Christ "who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption" (1:30). It is joined to "it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends" (2Co 10:18); What to boast in; "let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight" (Jer 9:24); The boast is in knowing God, and what is known is his character; The soul's boast. "My soul makes its boast in the Lord; let the humble hear and be glad" (Psa 34:2, carried); Not in my bow. "For not in my bow do I trust ... In God we have boasted continually" (Psa 44:6–8). The psalm then turns: "But you have rejected us" (44:9). The boast in God is kept in the psalm even while the defeat is brought before him; His name. "Glory in his holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice!" (Psa 105:3; 1Ch 16:10); The worm. "Fear not, you worm Jacob ... you shall rejoice in the Lord; in the Holy One of Israel you shall glory" (Isa 41:14–16). The one called a worm is the one who glories; Justified and glorying. "Only in the Lord, it shall be said of me, are righteousness and strength ... In the Lord all the offspring of Israel shall be justified and shall glory" (Isa 45:24–25); The nations. If Israel returns and swears in truth, "nations shall bless themselves in him, and in him shall they glory" (Jer 4:2); Exulting; "all who swear by him shall exult" (Psa 63:11); "Let the righteous one rejoice in the Lord and take refuge in him! Let all the upright in heart exult!" (Psa 64:10); "that I may glory with your inheritance" (Psa 106:5); The cross. "far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world" (Gal 6:14); Christ, not the flesh. "glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh — though I myself have reason for confidence in the flesh also" (Php 3:3–4). Paul has standing in the flesh, "I have more", and sets it aside; Hope, sufferings, God. ESV renders kauchaomai "rejoice" here:; "we rejoice in hope of the glory of God. Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings" (Rom 5:2–3); "we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation" (5:11); The same word that elsewhere is a proud boast is here joy in hope, in suffering, and in God; Held fast. "if indeed we hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope" (Heb 3:6); The conscience. "our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God" (2Co 1:12). The boast is a clear conscience, and its ground is named as grace.

15197.text: Paul's most frequent boast is in other people: "I have great pride in you; I am filled with comfort. In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy" (2Co 7:4); His boasts to Titus about them "proved true" (7:14). He asks them to "give proof ... of our boasting about you" (8:24). He sends brothers "so that our boasting about you may not prove empty" (9:3), or "we would be humiliated" (9:4). The boast puts Paul's own standing at risk on the conduct of others; "your readiness, of which I boast about you ... your zeal has stirred up most of them" (9:2); At Christ's coming; "what is our hope or joy or crown of boasting before our Lord Jesus at his coming? Is it not you?" (1Th 2:19); "on the day of our Lord Jesus you will boast of us as we will boast of you" (2Co 1:14); "so that in the day of Christ I may be proud that I did not run in vain" (Php 2:16); "we ourselves boast about you in the churches of God for your steadfastness and faith in all your persecutions" (2Th 1:4); "so that in me you may have ample cause to glory in Christ Jesus" (Php 1:26); His work, which is Christ's. "I have reason to be proud of my work for God. For I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me" (Rom 15:17–18). The pride is in a work he credits to Christ; "by my pride in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die every day!" (1Co 15:31); "Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation, and the rich in his humiliation" (Jam 1:9–10, carried).

15205.text: Proverbs paints the scoffer by what he will not receive: Rebuke; "A wise son hears his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke" (Pro 13:1); "A scoffer does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise" (15:12). The verse before is "Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the Lord; how much more the hearts of the children of man!" (15:11); Hatred of correction. "Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse ... Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you" (Pro 9:7–8). The same rebuke brings out hate in one and love in the other; Wisdom in vain. "A scoffer seeks wisdom in vain, but knowledge is easy for a man of understanding" (Pro 14:6). He seeks, and does not find; Learning by his fall; "Strike a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence" (19:25); "When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise" (21:11); The scoffer is not the one who learns. Others learn from what happens to him; Strife. "Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease" (Pro 22:10). "the scoffer is an abomination to mankind" (24:9); Justice and the guilt offering; "A worthless witness mocks at justice" (19:28). "Condemnation is ready for scoffers" (19:29); "Fools mock at the guilt offering, but the upright enjoy acceptance" (14:9). They mock the very means of putting guilt right; Delight, and the offer. "How long will scoffers delight in their scoffing ... If you turn at my reproof, behold, I will pour out my spirit to you" (Pro 1:22–23). Scoffing is a delight held on to, and the offer still stands to the one who turns; Alone. "If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it" (Pro 9:12); The seat. "Blessed is the man who ... nor sits in the seat of scoffers; but his delight is in the law of the Lord" (Psa 1:1–2). The scoffer's seat is set against delight in the law; The warning; "do not scoff, lest your bonds be made strong", then "Give ear, and hear my voice" (Isa 28:22–23). Again the opposite of scoffing is hearing; "the scoffer cease ... who by a word make a man out to be an offender, and lay a snare for him who reproves in the gate" (Isa 29:20–21). The scoffer works against the one who reproves. In the same passage "The meek shall obtain fresh joy in the Lord" (29:19); Wine and company; "Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise" (Pro 20:1); "the princes became sick with the heat of wine; he stretched out his hand with mockers", and "none of them calls upon me" (Hos 7:5, 7); In Job's debates; Zophar: "when you mock, shall no one shame you?" (Job 11:3); Job: "after I have spoken, mock on" (21:3); Elihu: "Beware lest wrath entice you into scoffing" (36:18); I read: the charge of scoffing is thrown between the speakers. As with Eliab in batch 2, the verses do not settle that it is true of Job; "Toward the scorners he is scornful, but to the humble he gives favor" (Pro 3:34, carried). This is the source of Jam 4:6 and 1Pe 5:5.

15247.text: The overview's surface pointer was a surface match only. The reading gives 42 pride-sense verses. Some surfaces such as "exalted" turned out to be God's or another's raising, so they are S or D (Isa 5:16, Isa 52:13, 2Ch 7:21, Act 13:17). Some plain surfaces such as "high" carry pride (Pro 17:19 "makes his door high", Psa 75:5, Isa 22:16).

15266.text: Turns toward help (Deu 33:26): Human pride: Turns away from God: "does not seek him" (Psa 10:4).

15288.text: H1363 gōbah: Gloss: height; Hits: 17; Verses: 16; Hits with a pride-like surface: 4 (Psa 10:4 and 2Ch 32:26 "pride"; Jer 48:29; Pro 16:18).

15332.text: It always faces someone: "before me" (1Ki 21:29); "before the Lord" (2Ki 22:19); "before the God of his fathers" (2Ch 33:12); "before your God" (Dan 10:12); Zedekiah's failure is put as "He did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke from the mouth of the Lord" (2Ch 36:12). Humbling before the prophet is humbling before the word he carries; Most verses in this group name before whom. Of the rest, 2Ch 12:6 and 2Ch 30:11 answer a word just brought, and Lev 26:41 goes with confession (26:40). Isa 58:3–5 is a fast addressed to God.

15336.text: What goes with it: saying "The Lord is righteous" (2Ch 12:6); tearing clothes, sackcloth, fasting, going about "dejectedly" (1Ki 21:27); weeping (2Ki 22:19); entreating and praying (2Ch 33:12–13); fasting and seeking (Ezr 8:21); the condition "humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways" (2Ch 7:14); confession, and making amends for iniquity (Lev 26:40–41).

15337.text: In Ezra the fast to humble themselves follows a choice not to lean on the king: "I was ashamed to ask the king for a band of soldiers … since we had told the king, 'The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him'" (Ezr 8:22).

15342.text: It does not last by itself. Of Rehoboam, two verses after his humbling: "he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the Lord" (2Ch 12:14).

15344.text: A humbling God does not take knowledge of: Isa 58:3–5: The people ask: "Why have we fasted, and you see it not? Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?"; The answer: "in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers", and "you fast only to quarrel and to fight"; The form is named and set aside: "Is it to bow down his head like a reed, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him?"; The fast God chooses is turned to others: "to loose the bonds of wickedness … to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, to cover him" (58:6–7); Compare Ahab. His sackcloth and fasting were seen and answered (1Ki 21:27–29); I read: the outward acts are the same. What differs, by the two passages, is what goes with them. Ahab acts "when Ahab heard those words", against himself. In Isa 58 the fast is kept alongside self-pleasure and oppression. The humbling that is not taken knowledge of is one that leaves the seen poor unseen (58:7). This joins OT-105; 10.1, 10.7 and 13.1 already cite Isa 58:3, 5. The reading here is for the humbling side.

15363.text: Dan 5:19: "whom he would, he raised up, and whom he would, he humbled". This is Nebuchadnezzar's power, "because of the greatness that he gave him" (5:18). The next verse turns it on him: "when his heart was lifted up … he was brought down" (5:20). The man who humbled whom he would was himself humbled.

15371.text: OT-103.44 (M02 × M09). 2Ch 12:7, 12:12 and 32:26 are read: humbling oneself turns God's wrath, in measure. Zep 2:3, Rom 13:5 and Job 40:11 are in this batch or later ones (Zep 2:3 is H6035, batch 2; Rom 13:5 is hypotassō, batch 5). The item stays narrowed until those are read.

15375.text: Already cited: 2Ch 12:7, 12:12, 32:26, 33:12 and 2Ki 22:19 (10.13, where humbling turns wrath); 2Ki 22:19, 2Ch 32:26 and Dan 5:19, 22 (Ch 4); Dan 4:17, 37 (13.1); Deu 8:3 (Ch 2); Pro 16:19 (Ch 12); 2Ch 7:14 (Ch 14); Isa 58:3, 5 (10.1, 10.7, 13.1). None is in a section about humbling, because there is none.

15377.text: H6031B ʿānāh (humble surface): Faces in batch 1: God humbles in testing (Deu 8) · humbling oneself by fasting (Ezr 8:21; Isa 58) · Pharaoh refuses to humble himself · humbled by God, then despised by men (Job 30:11) · the Philistines would humble Samson · Hagar told to submit; What differs: the same verb for God's testing, a person's fast, an enemy's binding and a servant's return. Its wider use ("afflict", 80 verses, M24) is not read here.

15384.text: The humble seek: "Seek the Lord, all you humble of the land, who do his just commands; seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the Lord" (Zep 2:3). Those already called humble are told to seek humility. I read: in this verse humility is not a thing held once and for all. The humble keep seeking it, under the threat of the day of anger (2:2); "I will leave in your midst a people humble and lowly. They shall seek refuge in the name of the Lord" (Zep 3:12). They are left after God removes "your proudly exultant ones" (3:11). They are described by what they do and do not do: "they shall do no injustice and speak no lies" (3:13); "The afflicted shall eat and be satisfied; those who seek him shall praise the Lord" (Psa 22:26) and "you who seek God, let your hearts revive" (Psa 69:32). In both, the humble or afflicted stand beside "those who seek". (Psa 22:26 is the afflicted sense, group VI.).

15385.text: The humble hear what God did for another, and are glad: "My soul makes its boast in the Lord; let the humble hear and be glad" (Psa 34:2). David's own deliverance follows: "I sought the Lord, and he answered me" (34:4). The superscription sets it after "he changed his behavior before Abimelech"; "When the humble see it they will be glad" (Psa 69:32). "It" is the deliverance of the speaker, who has said "I am afflicted and in pain" (69:29); I read: in both psalms, one man's boast is in the Lord, not in himself, and the humble are those who are glad at it. Their gladness is at what God did for someone else.

15389.text: The noun ʿănāwāh (H6038, M05 by tag) is in four of the five verses: Pro 15:33, 18:12, 22:4 and Zep 2:3.

15393.text: Set against religious acts in three passages: the fast (Isa 58:3–7, batch 1); offerings (Mic 6:6–8); the house and the sacrifices (Isa 66:1–3, group III).

15405.text: The seven verses decided "thread" are those where the verse is about the afflicted being oppressed or crying out. They are already coded in the poor/needy split (P or G) and carried by OT-105. Two of them name the heart: "you will strengthen their heart" (Psa 10:17), and "May your hearts live forever!" (Psa 22:26).

15425.text: afflicted: Verses: Psa 9:12; 10:12; 10:17; 22:26; Amo 2:7; Where the verse speaks of: their cry, their oppression, God not forgetting them.

15426.text: humble: Verses: Zep 2:3; Psa 25:9; 34:2; 69:32; 76:9; 147:6; 149:4; Pro 3:34; Where the verse speaks of: God's favor, teaching and saving, and their seeking and gladness.

15429.text: Psa 51:17: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.": What it is set against: "For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; you will not be pleased with a burnt offering" (51:16); What comes before: "Deliver me from bloodguiltiness" (51:14). The spirit and heart are broken over the speaker's own sin; What it is called: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit". It takes the place of the offering; The next verses: "then will you delight in right sacrifices" (51:19). The offerings are not abolished. They follow the broken heart; This is a fourth passage where what God looks to is set against a religious act. The others are Isa 58:3–7, Mic 6:6–8 and Isa 66:1–3 (batches 1 and 2). In Psa 51 the contrast is the speaker's own, and the next verses take it back up; "Contrite" here is H1794 (M10). "Broken" is H7665 (M24/T3). No M09 word is in the verse.

15479.text: M47 (#1979): Mat 11:29 (heart, souls), 1Pe 3:4 and 3:8 (heart), Jam 1:21 (souls), Jam 3:14 and 4:8 (hearts), Luk 1:51 (hearts). Checked at the cross-check.

15511.text: OT-103.44 (M02 × M09): Rom 13:5 is now read. Subjection "to avoid God's wrath but also for the sake of conscience".
