18709.text: H2416A with the divine party in 98 verses. Its commonest near pair is "alive + LORD" (64), e.g. 1Ki 17:1, 17:12, 18:10. This points to the oath "as the LORD lives". It is a pointer only; reading would confirm it.

18749.text: spirit: Pro 20:27 ("the spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD")

18793.text: Face: F. Breath that understands and speaks; Hits / verses: 3 / 3; What differs: The breath as the source of understanding and words; Example verses: Job 32:8; Pro 20:27; Job 26:4

18799.text: Face: M. The inner person revived; Hits / verses: 11 / 10; What differs: Spirit, heart and soul revived or living; a people revived; Example verses: Isa 57:15; Psa 69:32; 22:26; Isa 55:3; Gen 45:27

18801.text: Face: O. Live by doing God's word; Hits / verses: 25 / 24; What differs: Life tied to statutes, justice, wisdom, seeking him, faith; Example verses: Lev 18:5; Deu 8:3; 30:19; Amo 5:4; Hab 2:4

18813.text: "To live" (H2421) moves between: duration ("lived 930 years"); survival ("that we may live and not die"); being let live by another (Exo 1; Jos 9); recovery from sickness; the return of life to the dead (1Ki 17; 2Ki 13); the revival of spirit, heart and soul (Isa 57:15; Psa 69:32); life given by the word and asked for in prayer (Psa 119); life as the outcome of turning (Eze 18; 33); What differs is what life is set against. It may be set against death by hunger, a sword, sickness, a crushed spirit or a heart worn down, or against "the death of the wicked". The word does not change; what threatens it does. *(R: I read the contrast from the verse's own pairing, e.g. "that we may live and not die", "turn, and live … why will you die".)*

18814.text: "Breath" (H5397 / H5301 / H6315) has four faces: life given (Gen 2:7); understanding (Job 32:8; Pro 20:27); force and wrath (Job 4:9); what a person breathes out: lies, contempt, longing (Pro 14:5; Psa 10:5; Psa 12:5); The same breath that God gives comes back out as lies or longing. *(R: the verbs are the same root group, but no verse sets them side by side; this is noted as a range of the word, not as a teaching.)*

18818.text: Q3 The heart after death.; Unit 1 has no verse on the heart after death.; The nearest are the living heart revived (Isa 57:15; Psa 69:32) and the wish "May your hearts live forever!" (Psa 22:26), which is not about death.; A focused pull (heart with die, death or Sheol) is needed before anything is said.

18831.text: 1Ki 1:2 (M47 "bosom") | M47 batch H: *"the king's failing body"* | The servants arrange for the king. | Considered. The king is the setting.

18835.text: 1. Where the authority comes from: Pilate (Joh 19:10–11): *"So Pilate said to him, 'You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?' Jesus answered him, 'You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above. Therefore he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin.'"*; The passage before: *"When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid"* (19:8), after *"he has made himself the Son of God"* (19:7). He asks *"Where are you from?"*, and Jesus gives *"no answer"* (19:9). After: *"From then on Pilate sought to release him"*, and then the cry, *"you are not Caesar's friend"* (19:12).

18836.text: Reading: Pilate speaks of his authority when he is afraid (19:8) and has had no answer (19:9). He states it twice, release and crucify. Jesus does not deny it. He names its source, "given you from above", and that changes how guilt is weighed: "therefore" the one who handed him over has the greater sin. After this Pilate seeks to release him, and the crowd moves him with another authority, Caesar's (19:12).

18837.text: Home: Ch 11 §7, under a new face, *where authority comes from*. 10.12 *Fear* (19:8, 12): fear acting through the one in authority. 13.1 for "given you from above", as God's character only.

18841.text: Placement now: not cited (Rom 7 is in 10.7 *Willing*). Home: Ch 11 §7, with a pointer to 10.7 (Rom 7:15–21, a will that is not master) and Ch 14.

18864.text: Counted, not assumed: "used five times" (losing heart). *kāʾāh* has 3 verses, *kāʾeh* 1 and *athumeō* 1 in iba.db verse_lexical.; "Where the verses tell a person not to be anxious, they never leave it there." Checked against all 9 commands in the set: Mat 6:25, 31, 34; Luk 12:22, 29; Mat 10:19; Luk 12:11; Phili 4:6; 1Pe 5:7.; "In several of these scenes" (perplexity). It ends with someone arriving in 5 of the 11 verses: Luk 24:4; Act 5:24–25; Act 2:14; Act 10:17–19; Dan 5:12.

18872.text: Reverse audit (style guide §8.1). Every phenomenon §1–§16 has a placement, and the woven ones carry their key verses. 10.1, 10.2, 10.5 and 10.9 do not reproduce v3's seat blocks. Where a seat block says something about the inner being, it is carried as a verse in the account, for example Psa 13:2, 102:4, 69:20, 51:10–11, 27:8 and Dan 11:28. The seat analysis itself stays in v3.

18878.text: Hiding from people: Much of the hiding in Scripture is from people who could do harm, and in these verses it is the weaker side that hides. "When the wicked rise, people hide themselves" (Proverbs 28:28). "The poor of the earth all hide themselves" (Job 24:4). When Israel hid in the caves, "all the people followed him trembling" (1 Samuel 13:7).; Often the verse records not the feeling of the one who hides but someone else's counsel to hide.; Jonathan: "Saul my father seeks to kill you … Stay in a secret place and hide yourself" (1 Samuel 19:2).; God to Elijah: "hide yourself by the brook Cherith" (1 Kings 17:3).; Where the feeling is named, it is fear.; Jacob fled from Laban "secretly", and he said why: "Because I was afraid" (Genesis 31:27, 31).; Joseph of Arimathea was "a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews". The same verse ends with him going to Pilate and taking away the body (John 19:38).; Hiding can be good sense: "The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it" (Proverbs 22:3). It ends when the news changes. The men who had hidden in the hills "heard that the Philistines were fleeing, they too followed hard after them in the battle" (1 Samuel 14:22).; And sometimes hiding is refused, or impossible.; The servant chooses not to hide: "I gave my back to those who strike … I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting" (Isaiah 50:6).; No one can hide from a friend who turns: "it is not an adversary who deals insolently with me — then I could hide from him. But it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend" (Psalm 55:12–13).

18889.text: The hidden trap: In the Psalms a purpose is hidden in order to catch someone. "They hold fast to their evil purpose; they talk of laying snares secretly, thinking, 'Who can see them?'" (Psalm 64:5). The next verse says where the purpose was hidden first: "For the inward mind and heart of a man are deep" (64:6).; The one it is set for prays out of his weakness. "When my spirit faints within me, you know my way! In the path where I walk they have hidden a trap for me" (Psalm 142:3). "No one cares for my soul" (142:4). It is worse when it comes from those he had prayed for: "Yet they have dug a pit for my life. Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them" (Jeremiah 18:20).; And the trap turns. "In the net that they hid, their own foot has been caught" (Psalm 9:15). The soul the pit was dug for (Psalm 35:7) is the soul that rejoices: "Then my soul will rejoice in the Lord" (35:9). The one taken "out of the net they have hidden for me" says, "Into your hand I commit my spirit" (Psalm 31:4–5).

18895.text: Ch 12: the hidden trap and the deep heart (Psa 64:6; 140:2); concealed wrong.

18902.text: | 2Ch 22:9, "heart" | the heart is Jehoshaphat's, not the one hiding

18905.text: What carries it instead of a seat: the question spoken aloud: "What does this mean?" (Act 2:12); "who is this about whom I hear such things?" (Luk 9:9, context); the gaze: "The disciples looked at one another" (Joh 13:22); a reflexive pronoun: Act 10:17 "inwardly perplexed" is *en heautō*, "in himself". The inner location is there, but through a pronoun, not a seat word.; the body of the other party: in Dan 5:6 the king's "color changed … his limbs gave way, and his knees knocked together". The body tells the alarm while his lords are perplexed.

18925.text: *satar* H5641, hide (75 no-seat) | Psa 143:7 "my spirit fails! Hide not your face"; Psa 88:14 soul; Psa 104:29 "they are dismayed … breath"; Psa 10:11 heart | God hiding his face. The seat is the human recipient's: Psa 13:1 (13:2 "sorrow in my heart"); Psa 30:7 "you hid your face; I was dismayed"; Psa 44:24; 69:17; 102:2; Isa 8:17 ("I will wait … and I will hope in him"); Isa 54:8; 59:2; 64:7; Mic 3:4; Deu 31:17 | Physical hiding (David 1Sa 20, 23, 26; Jeremiah and Baruch Jer 36): outward, with inner being behind the act at most. God concealing (Pro 25:2; Deu 29:29): divine subject

18928.text: *merimnaō* G3309, be anxious (15) | Mat 6:25 / Luk 12:22 *psychē*; 1Cor 7:34 "holy in body and spirit" | Discourse-level seat: Mat 6:27–34; Luk 12:25–26; 1Cor 7:32–33. The seat arrives after the handing-over: Phili 4:6 "do not be anxious" → 4:7 "the peace of God … will guard your hearts and your minds" | The same word has opposite value: 1Cor 12:25 "the same care for one another" and Phili 2:20 "genuinely concerned for your welfare" are positive, relational concern. Luk 10:41, Martha: the seat is absent; the doubled name carries the Lord's address

18933.text: 3. What carries the inner being when there is no seat (M20): The operation word names itself. *Perplexed, doubted, anxious, discouraged* need no seat. The seat is added when someone diagnoses (Luk 24:38) or sets the frame of a discourse (Mat 6:25; Luk 12:22).; The act carries it. Hiding for fear; the sluggard's buried hand (§1.5; §2 *taman*).; The body carries it. Peter sinking; Belshazzar's knees; bread eaten with trembling (§1.2; §1.1; §2).; Speech carries it. The grumblers' quoted words; "What does this mean?"; the father's "What shall I do about my son?" (§1.6; §1.1; §2).; The seat is inside the word. *Dipsuchos*, *athumeō*, *alupos*, and brokenhearted *ka'ah* (§1.3).; Inner places named outside M47: "bosom" H2243 T2 (Job 31:33: ESV "heart" is *chob*); "chambers of the belly" (Pro 18:8); "in himself" (Act 10:17); These are seats the M47 list does not hold.; The passage carries it. The seat is stated once and inherited (Luk 12; Mat 6), stated as the cause in the next clause (Deu 1:28), or given as the passage's frame (Jer 17:5–10; 2Cor 4:6, 16).; Another party's seat. Jesus troubled in spirit while the disciples are perplexed (Joh 13:21–22); the oppressor's heart and the victim's crushing (Psa 10:10–11); God hides his face and the human is dismayed (Psa 30:7).; No inner operation at all. Physical concealment of objects and people, and "cut off". This is the largest single group, and the tag does not describe it.

18954.text: Indecency, exposure (M53 E). H6172 *ʿerwāh* "nakedness" (T2; "indecent" in Deu 23:14; 24:1), G0809 *aschēmōn* "unpresentable" (T2, 1Co 12:23), G1570 *ekthetos* "exposed" (T2), H1540I *gālāh* "uncover" (T3).: Points that follow from the scan, with no reading done:

18960.text: They sit in the same verses and passages. Verb and noun share 4 verses and come within three verses of each other in 9: Goliath (1Sa 17:25–26), Psa 44:13–16, Psa 69:6–10, Psa 79:12, Psa 89:50–51, Psa 119:39–42, Zep 2:8–10. Rom 15:3 quotes Psa 69:9 with both Greek words: "The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me."

18961.text: The same verses also carry M07's shame words. Psa 44:15 "All day long my disgrace is before me, and shame has covered my face", next to the taunter of 44:16. Psa 69:6–7 "let not those who hope in you be put to shame … dishonor has covered my face", before 69:9. 1Pe 4:14 "if you are insulted for the name of Christ" is two verses from 4:16 "let him not be ashamed". 1Co 4:12 "when reviled, we bless" sits between "we in disrepute" (4:10) and "I do not write these things to make you ashamed" (4:14).

19026.text: The manner forbidden: ruthlessly, harshly, with force (Lev 25; Eze 34:4); domineering (1Pe 5:3); lording it (Mat 20:25; 2Cor 1:24).

19038.text: The passage. Dathan and Abiram refuse twice: *"We will not come up"* (16:12, 14). Moses before this, to Korah: *"would you seek the priesthood also?"* (16:10). After: *"Moses was very angry and said to the Lord, 'Do not respect their offering. I have not taken one donkey from them'"* (16:15).

19070.text: The passage. *"the fear of them had fallen on all peoples"* (9:2). *"the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them"* (9:3; in 10.10).

19108.text: Eze 34:4. *"The weak you have not strengthened, the sick you have not healed, the injured you have not bound up, the strayed you have not brought back, the lost you have not sought, and with force and harshness you have ruled them."*

19162.text: Ezra 8. The hand brings him the men he needed (8:18). He will not ask the king for soldiers; because he has said, "The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him" (8:22). 8:21–22 are in; 10.14.

19166.text: 10.7 *Choosing and setting direction*: Ezra 7:10, setting the heart to study, do and teach. It is; a clear verse for the heart's direction, and it is not in the book. Rehoboam, who "did not set his; heart to seek the Lord" (2 Chronicles 12:14), is in 10.13 and 10.14, and is its opposite.

19167.text: 10.12 *Fear*, "What changes it", or 10.9: Ezra 7:28, courage taken *because* God's hand is on; him. Ezra 8:22 already shows Ezra choosing not to lean on the king's soldiers. 7:28 gives the inner; ground.

19193.text: (a) The fugitive hunted to death.; Verses: 1Sa 19:2; 20:5, 19, 24; 23:19, 23; 26:1; Psa 54:1 (David); Judg 9:5 (Jotham); 2Sa 17:9 (David, as Hushai pictures him); 1Ki 17:3 (Elijah); Jer 36:19 (Baruch and Jeremiah); Jos 2:16 (the spies); Jos 10:16, 17, 27 (five kings); 2Ch 22:9 (Ahaziah); Joh 8:59; 12:36 (Jesus).; Where it comes from: a stated threat to life. "Saul my father seeks to kill you" (1Sa 19:2); Abimelech "killed his brothers … But Jotham … hid himself" (Judg 9:5); "they picked up stones to throw at him" (Joh 8:59).; The feeling of the one who hides is almost never stated. What is stated is someone else's counsel to hide: Jonathan (1Sa 19:2), Rahab (Jos 2:16), the officials (Jer 36:19), and God (1Ki 17:3). In this strand the inner operation that shows is the counsellor's: foresight and concern for the other.; What it leads to: survival (Jotham; David), or capture and death (Ahaziah, "captured while hiding", 2Ch 22:9; the five kings, Jos 10:17, 27).

19201.text: Seat.; In the verse: 2Ch 22:9 "heart". The word has a genuine inner-being sense, but the heart is Jehoshaphat's, the dead grandfather's: "who sought the Lord with all his heart". Ahaziah, the one hiding, has no seat. Spurious for this phenomenon (v1 §0). Batch C v3 §7.1 read it as seeking the Lord with the heart. Batch G v3 §16.11 read it as "a dead man honoured for his grandfather's heart". Both readings stand. Neither concerns hiding.; Whose seat: none of the 40 hiders has one. In strand (a) the inner operation belongs to the counsellor, and it is shown by what the counsellor says, not by a seat word (v2, kept above).; Outside the verse — new in v3. In strand (a), the nearest seat word is *nephesh* in its life sense: the life being hunted. David, in the psalm headed by the Ziphites' report that he is "hiding among us" (Psa 54:1), says "the Lord is the upholder of my life" (54:4). The seat word names what is at stake in the hiding, not where the hider feels it. This fits Batch G v3 §5 ("Life spared, life hunted — the *nephesh* as a prize"), which it does not change.; Strand (f), prudence — new in v3: Pro 22:3 ("The prudent sees danger and hides himself") → 22:5 "Thorns and snares are in the way of the crooked; whoever guards his soul will keep far from them". The prudent one's hiding is a guarding of the soul. *Nephesh* here is the self that is kept from harm, and it passes the check in that sense. Strand (f) is the only strand of §2 where the one who hides has a seat, and the seat is the thing the hiding protects.

19203.text: God hiding the person: "hide me in the shadow of your wings" (Psa 17:8); "he will hide me in his shelter in the day of trouble" (Psa 27:5); "you hide them from the plots of men; you store them … from the strife of tongues" (Psa 31:20); "Hide me from the secret plots of the wicked" (Psa 64:2); "You shall be hidden from the lash of the tongue" (Job 5:21); "the Lord hid them" (Jer 36:26); "in the shadow of his hand he hid me … in his quiver he hid me away" (Isa 49:2): hidden for later use, not only for safety; "enter your chambers … hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by" (Isa 26:20): God's own people hidden from God's own fury; "perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the Lord" (Zep 2:3): conditional, after "seek humility"; "your life is hidden with Christ in God" (Col 3:3), after "Set your minds on things that are above" (3:2)

19212.text: What it does in the human: Dismay: "you hid your face; I was dismayed" (Psa 30:7); "When you hide your face, they are dismayed; when you take away their breath, they die" (Psa 104:29); The spirit failing: "My spirit fails! Hide not your face from me, lest I be like those who go down to the pit" (Psa 143:7); Being cast away: "why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face" (Psa 88:14); Feeling forgotten: "Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?" (Psa 13:1). The seat follows at once: "How long must I take counsel in my soul and have sorrow in my heart all the day?" (13:2); The body pressed down: "Why do you hide your face? … For our soul is bowed down to the dust; our belly clings to the ground" (Psa 44:24–25); Melting: "you have hidden your face from us, and have made us melt in the hand of our iniquities" (Isa 64:7). The previous verse: "We all fade like a leaf" (64:6); Being counted an enemy: "Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?" (Job 13:24); "Will you frighten a driven leaf?" (13:25); A collective conclusion: "Have not these evils come upon us because our God is not among us?" (Deu 31:17); Complaint: "My way is hidden from the Lord, and my right is disregarded by my God" (Isa 40:27). The answer: "He does not faint or grow weary … He gives power to the faint" (40:28–29); Banishment and the fear that follows it: Cain, "from your face I shall be hidden. I shall be a fugitive … whoever finds me will kill me" (Gen 4:14), after "My punishment is greater than I can bear" (4:13). Being hidden from God's face is followed at once by fear of man.

19219.text: What it does. The same fact works in opposite directions, depending on who is seen: Comfort for the sufferer: "all my longing is before you; my sighing is not hidden from you" (Psa 38:9), between "the tumult of my heart" (38:8) and "My heart throbs" (38:10); Confession for the penitent: "you know my folly; the wrongs I have done are not hidden from you" (Psa 69:5); Wonder at being known before birth: "My frame was not hidden from you, when I was being made in secret" (Psa 139:15); Judgement for the evildoer: "They are not hidden from me, nor is their iniquity concealed" (Jer 16:17); "Israel is not hidden from me; for now, O Ephraim, you have played the whore" (Hos 5:3); "There is no gloom or deep darkness where evildoers may hide themselves" (Job 34:22); "Can a man hide himself in secret places so that I cannot see him? … Do I not fill heaven and earth?" (Jer 23:24); "If they hide themselves on the top of Carmel … at the bottom of the sea …" (Amo 9:3)

19234.text: What it leads to, in the person. Fear to ask (Luk 9:45); a plea, "I am a sojourner on the earth; hide not your commandments from me!" (Psa 119:19); searching, "the glory of kings is to search things out" (Pro 25:2); obedience to what is revealed, "the things that are revealed belong to us … that we may do all the words of this law" (Deu 29:29). Job 3:23, "a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in", is the not-knowing that hems in.

19237.text: Where it comes from. Something heard or seen that exceeds the categories at hand: "it was said by some that John had been raised from the dead" (Luk 9:7); "we hear them telling in our own tongues" (Act 2:11–12); "what the vision … might mean" (Act 10:17); an empty tomb (Luk 24:3–4); Jesus's "one of you will betray me" (Joh 13:21–22); writing on a wall no one could read (Dan 5:8–9)

19238.text: What it does. It asks aloud: "What does this mean?" (Act 2:12); "who is this about whom I hear such things?" (Luk 9:9). It looks at others: "The disciples looked at one another" (Joh 13:22). It turns inward: "Peter was inwardly [*en heautō*, in himself] perplexed" (Act 10:17). Festus hands the question on: "Being at a loss how to investigate … I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem" (Act 25:20).

19240.text: What it leads to. Mostly, something from outside ends it: "While they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them" (Luk 24:4); "the men … stood at the gate" and "the Spirit said to him" (Act 10:17, 19); "Peter, standing with the eleven, lifted up his voice" (Act 2:14); the queen names Daniel (Dan 5:10–12); Herod "sought to see him" (Luk 9:9); Perplexity ends when an interpreter or a meeting arrives.

19246.text: (a) Anxiety over provision (Mat 6:25, 27, 28, 31, 34; Luk 12:22, 25, 26, 29).; Where from: "what you will eat or what you will drink … what you will put on" (Mat 6:25).; What it does: nothing. "which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?" (6:27 = Luk 12:25). It multiplies itself forward: "tomorrow will be anxious for itself" (6:34). It suspends the person: *meteōrizō*, "be held in suspense" (Luk 12:29).; What it co-exists with: "little faith" (Luk 12:28), and the Gentiles' seeking (Mat 6:32).; What displaces it: looking at birds and lilies (6:26, 28); knowing "your heavenly Father knows that you need them" (6:32); "seek first the kingdom" (6:33).; The seat is stated once, at the head: "anxious about your life [*psychē*]" (Mat 6:25; Luk 12:22). The rest of the discourse inherits it.

19249.text: (d) Care for others, valued as good.; "I have no one like him, who will be genuinely concerned for your welfare" (Phili 2:20), against "they all seek their own interests" (2:21).; "the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches" (2Cor 11:28). The next verse shows what that anxiety is: "Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to fall, and I am not indignant?" (11:29). Anxiety for others is sharing in their condition.; "the members may have the same care for one another" (1Cor 12:25).; "that I may be less anxious" (Phili 2:28), in a chain of feeling between Epaphroditus, Paul and the Philippians (2:26–28).; A father: Kish "anxious about you, saying, 'What shall I do about my son?'" (1Sa 10:2). His care shifts from the donkeys to the son (9:5; 10:2).; The same word *merimnaō* carries (a) and (d). Its value depends on its object: self-provision against others' welfare.

19251.text: (f) Anxiety handed over or answered.; "do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God" (Phili 4:6) → "the peace of God … will guard your hearts and your minds" (4:7); "casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you" (1Pe 5:7); "When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul" (Psa 94:19); "Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad" (Pro 12:25); "Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts [*sar'appim*, anxious thoughts]" (Psa 139:23); The movement: anxiety is given to another, or answered by a word, and becomes peace or gladness. The seat is named where the anxiety sits (heart) and where the answer lands (soul, hearts and minds).

19254.text: The one who is not anxious. "He is like a tree planted by water … does not fear when heat comes … is not anxious in the year of drought" (Jer 17:8). He is "the man who trusts in the Lord" (17:7), and the passage then turns to "The heart is deceitful … I the Lord search the heart" (17:9–10).

19255.text: Seat. Anxiety holds the most in-verse seats of any M20 phenomenon (8 of 30). The seat word plays three different roles, and v3 separates them.; The seat as where the anxiety sits (bearer's own, genuine): Pro 12:25 "Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down" (strand f). Batch A v3 §6 ("Anxiety in the heart").; Luk 21:34 "lest your hearts be weighed down with … cares of this life" (strand e). Batch A v3 §6.; Psa 139:23 "know my heart! … know my thoughts [anxious thoughts]" (strand f). Batch A v3 §6 ("God searching the anxious heart").; The seat as where the answer lands (bearer's own, genuine): Psa 94:19 "your consolations cheer my soul" (strand f). Batch A v3 §6 notes that "heart" in this verse is English only. New in v3 [lexical]: the Hebrew locates the cares "within me" (*beqirbi*) and names the *nephesh* only at the receiving end. In Hebrew, the seat is named where the consolation arrives, not where the anxiety sits.; Phili 4:6 → 4:7 "will guard your hearts and your minds" (v1 §2 *merimnaō* row).; The seat as the object the anxiety is about (bearer's own, but not its location): Mat 6:25; Luk 12:22 "do not be anxious about your life [*psychē*] … nor about your body". Batch A v3 §6 ("Anxiety about life (psychē) and body"). New in v3, seat-sense: *psychē* here is the life that needs food. The next verse puts it so: "For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing" (Luk 12:23). The seat word is what the anxiety is about, not where it happens. The whole discourse inherits this frame (v1 §1.4: "discourse-level seat").; 1Cor 7:34 "anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit" (strand c). Batch A v3 §6 ("Divided interests") [H]. New in v3: here too the spirit is the object of the care, what she wants to be holy, and the care has a good aim. Within strand (c), the seat is on the undivided side of the divided care.; The seat as what dread displaces (the dreader's own, genuine): Isa 57:11 "did not lay it to heart". Batch D v2 §4.6 ("fear → lying → not laying to heart"). New in v3: the heart is not where the dread sits. It is the place God should have been set, and dread took that place instead.; Outside the verse, other seats in the strands:

19256.text: Strand (b), a divine Spirit replaces the anxious speaker's own seat. Mat 10:19 → 10:20 "it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you". Batch E v2 §1.6 ("The Spirit speaks through the person"). The anxiety about what to say is answered by another's Spirit in the speaker's place. The Luke parallel runs the same way: Luk 12:11 → 12:12 "for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say". Luke gives the answer as teaching: the Spirit supplies the knowing that the anxiety lacked.; Strand (e), the choked hearer is set between two hearts — new in v3. Luk 8:14 (the thorns) stands between "the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts" (8:12) and "hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience" (8:15). The cares act on a heart where the word has been sown, and the contrast the passage draws is with a good heart that holds the word fast. Mat 13:22 ← 13:19 "snatches away what has been sown in his heart" is the same frame (v1 §2 *merimna* row).; The man who is not anxious. Jer 17:8 is framed by "whose heart turns away from the Lord" (17:5), and by "The heart is deceitful … I the Lord search the heart and test the mind" (17:9–10) (v1 §2 *de'agah* row). The unanxious tree stands between two statements about the heart.; Strand (g), a neighbouring oracle's heart. Jer 49:23 (Hamath and Arpad "melt in fear, they are troubled like the sea") follows 49:22, the end of the oracle against Edom: "the heart of the warriors of Edom shall be in that day like the heart of a woman in her birth pains". The party is different: Edom in 49:22, the cities of Damascus in 49:23. So the seat does not belong to the anxious ones of 49:23. What the two oracles share is the same collapse under bad news. It is stated as a heart in labour for Edom's warriors, and as melting and a troubled sea for Hamath. It is recorded as a parallel, not as the seat of 49:23.; Spurious context link: Jer 38:19 → 38:17 "your life shall be spared". *Nephesh* is bodily life here: the life Zedekiah fears to lose. It names what the dread is about, not a seat.

19271.text: The one who lays it.; "They hold fast to their evil purpose; they talk of laying snares secretly, thinking, 'Who can see them?'" (Psa 64:5). The next verse gives the depth: "For the inward mind and heart of a man are deep" (64:6). The concealment is of intent, and the heart is its hiding place.; Also: "The arrogant have hidden a trap for me" (Psa 140:5); "without cause they hid their net for me" (35:7); "they have dug a pit to take me and laid snares for my feet" (Jer 18:22).

19274.text: What it leads to. The trap turns on its maker (Psa 9:15; 35:8), or God is the refuge from it (31:4). The seat appears on both sides: the trapper's deep heart (64:6), and the victim's fainting spirit and threatened life (142:3; 35:7).

19294.text: Psa 27:8–9: the heart seeks the face → "Hide not your face" (v3)

19303.text: Two phenomena face each other in one psalm: "he will hide me in his shelter" (Psa 27:5) and "Hide not your face from me" (27:9). The same verb gives safety (§3) and dread (§5), depending on whether God hides the person or hides himself from the person. v3 adds that the heart between them, "My heart says to you, 'Your face, Lord, do I seek'" (27:8), is seeking the face.

19308.text: 2Ch 22:9 | "heart" *levav* (H3824) | HS §2 | a third party's (Jehoshaphat) | genuine, but spurious for the hider | v1 §0; C v3 §7.1; G v3 §16.11

19316.text: Psa 139:23 | "heart" *levav* (H3824) | AX §11 | bearer's own | genuine | A v3 §6

19328.text: Zec 11:16 | "flesh" *basar* (H1320) | NO §17 | none | spurious: flesh as food | v1 §2

19341.text: Spurious for the phenomenon | Gen 3:8; Exo 16:8; 2Ch 22:9; Zec 11:9; Zec 11:16; Rev 2:17 | 6

19342.text: What the map shows across the phenomena.: Where the genuine seats fall: on the one who suffers the phenomenon (FH, AX, TR, LH); on the one who causes or misreads it (FH, CD, and in context TR and LH); on an interpreter or diagnoser (PX Dan 5:12, UC Luk 9:47, both in context); The concealment phenomena that are outward acts (HG, HS, SH) have no genuine seat in-verse at all. In context, their nearest seat word is the life that is hunted (Psa 54:4) or the heart that melted into confession (Jos 2:11).; The seat word does four jobs in M20, and only one is "where the phenomenon sits": the location (Pro 12:25; Psa 143:7); the object (Mat 6:25; 1Cor 7:34); the landing place of the answer (Psa 94:19; Phili 4:7); the site of the remedy (Jam 4:8; Psa 51:10); The seat often comes one verse away, and the direction matters: before the phenomenon, as its cause or ground (Psa 27:8; Deu 1:28; Isa 29:13; Isa 54:6; Dan 11:27); after it, as its experience, its diagnosis, or its answer (Psa 13:2; 69:20; 102:4; Luk 9:47; Phili 4:7; Psa 31:5–7; 35:9; 22:26); The seat of the one who does *not* undergo the phenomenon sometimes stands beside it: Caleb's "different spirit" among the grumblers (Num 14:24); the prudent one who "guards his soul" (Pro 22:5); Daniel's "excellent spirit" among the perplexed (Dan 5:12). The seat is named in the contrast figure, not in the crowd.; Concealment of the heart behind speech or act recurs outside §7: the trapper's heart (Psa 64:6; 140:2), the whisperer's glazed lips over an evil heart (Pro 26:23, 25), the aggressor's heart set before the act (Dan 11:28). In these phenomena the hidden thing is the heart itself.

19344.text: Psa 22:24 (FH) | Psa 22:26 "May your hearts live forever!" | bearers' own · genuine | §5 Seat

19363.text: §5 refines v1 §2's "implicit seat" for *satar*. The seat falls on the human who bears God's hiddenness. v1's statement stands, and §5 gives its detail. v3 adds the offender's heart that does not feel it (Isa 57:17) and the heart that seeks the face (Psa 27:8).

19402.text: 10 of the 29 marked M64 × M47 verses (m64-m47-marked-verses-v1-20261006) are in this set: Lev 7:18, 1Ki 12:33, Neh 6:8, Psa 17:3, Psa 35:4, Dan 6:3, Jon 1:4, Act 11:23, 1Co 4:5 and 2Co 1:17.

19406.text: Isaiah 65:12 — "chose what I did not delight in": This is an oracle. It opens with God, not with the people: *"I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me … I said, “Here I am, here I am,”"* (v1); *"I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, following their own devices"* (v2); The wrong choosing in v12 is made in front of a God who is calling and holding out his hands.; The oracle shows what they turned to instead: sacrifices *"in gardens"*, sitting *"in tombs"*, eating *"pig’s flesh"* (v3–4); a pride that says *"do not come near me, for I am too holy for you"* (v5); they *"forget my holy mountain"* and *"set a table for Fortune and fill cups of mixed wine for Destiny"* (v11); They put their trust in luck and fate.; The answer turns on their own word: *"I will destine you to the sword"* (v12). In Hebrew, "Destiny" (Meni, H4507) and "destine" (manah, H4487) come from the same root. They poured cups for Destiny, and the Lord destines them. What they chose to trust becomes the form their judgement takes.; The verse then gives the reason, and the reason is in the inner being: *"because, when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in."* The choosing does not stand alone. It is the far end of not answering and not listening. When they turned away from the voice calling them, that was already a choice, and choosing what God does not delight in is where it ends.; There is a phrase to set beside Joshua 24. There, the choice turned on what was *"evil in your eyes"*. Here they *"did what was evil in my eyes"*. The measure has moved from their eyes to God's, and his delight is the standard their choice is judged by.; In the same oracle the word "chosen" is used of the others: *"my chosen shall possess it"* (v9); *"You shall leave your name to my chosen for a curse"* (v15); So in one passage there are those who chose what God did not delight in, and those God calls *"my chosen"*. The outcome sets the two side by side and reaches the inner being on both sides: *"my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit"* (v14). The choice ends in the heart and spirit of the one who made it.

19415.text: 1.6 Plans for welfare, and thought for the one in need: *"For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope"* (Jer 29:11).; The verse looks ahead to *"When seventy years are completed"* (29:10).; It is followed by *"You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart"* (29:13).; *"As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me"* (Psa 40:17).; *"But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast"* (2Sa 14:14). The wise woman says it against the fact that *"We must all die"*.

19418.text: 1.9 The Spirit intercedes according to the will of God, and the purpose is turned toward those who love him: *"Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God"* (Rom 8:26–27).; The Spirit's praying is matched to God's will, and the one who searches hearts knows the Spirit's mind.; The meaning of "mind" (G5427) is left as Paul gives it: OT-94, which comes back with M63.; The next verse goes straight on: *"And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose"* (Rom 8:28).

19423.text: Seeking: after his plans for welfare, *"when you seek me with all your heart"* (Jer 29:13).

19428.text: 3. Placement: All 31 verses are placed in 13.1 v6.; v1 kept Rom 8:27 out as a Holy Spirit verse.; The researcher ruled that for 13.1 the Spirit is part of the divine (2026-10-08, quoted above), so in v2 it is placed with 8:26 in §1.9.

19501.text: Know and serve with the whole inner being. *"know the God of your father and serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind, for the Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought"* (1Ch 28:9).

19508.text: A condition. *"I will establish his kingdom forever if he continues strong in keeping my commandments"* (1Ch 28:7); *"if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever"* (28:9).

19592.text: Led to: Wisdom's call to *"simple ones"* and *"fools"* (v5), and her words: *"all straight to him who understands, and right to those who find knowledge"* (v9).

19606.text: Psalm 105:43: "his chosen ones with singing": Psalm 105 is a call to remember. It is addressed to the chosen: *"Remember the wondrous works that he has done … O offspring of Abraham, his servant, children of Jacob, his chosen ones!"* (v5–6). It starts with the heart: *"let the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice!"* (v3).; The psalm's reason is God's own remembering: *"He remembers his covenant forever"* (v8); *"For he remembered his holy promise, and Abraham, his servant"* (v42); The verse follows straight on: *"So he brought his people out with joy, his chosen ones with singing"* (v43). The joy and singing are set on the people brought out. They come with being brought out, and the bringing out comes from God remembering his promise. The chosen are told to remember (v5) because he remembered (v8, v42).; On the way there the psalm tells one man's inward testing: *"His feet were hurt with fetters … until what he had said came to pass, the word of the Lord tested him"* (v18–19). That man was Joseph, sent ahead of the chosen.; Psalm 105 tells nothing of the people's failures. It has *"none among his tribes who stumbled"* (v37). Its last verse states the purpose of the whole: *"that they might keep his statutes and observe his laws"* (v45).

19613.text: Being chosen is not a guarantee. This is stated in the verses, not inferred: the condition put on Solomon, and the *"cast you off forever"* (1Ch 28:7, 9); the chosen people's forgetting, craving, jealousy and unbelief, and their despising the land (Psa 106:7–43); the chosen people weary of God, and not calling on him (Isa 43:22–24); In Psalm 106:24 the chosen *"despised"* (H3988A) what was given. This is the same word as the refusing in §2a.

19621.text: Numbers 17:5: "Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel": The verse closes a long dispute over who God has chosen. It begins in Numbers 16. Korah and 250 chiefs, *"chosen from the assembly, well-known men"* (16:2; *qārîʾ*, H7148, "called"), rise up: *"Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the Lord?"* (16:3). Moses answers with God's choosing: *"The one whom he chooses he will bring near to him"* (16:5), and *"the man whom the Lord chooses shall be the holy one"* (16:7).; Moses names what is underneath the complaint: *"is it too small a thing for you that the God of Israel has separated you … And would you seek the priesthood also?"* (16:9–10). What they already have is not enough. They seek more.; *"Therefore it is against the Lord that you and all your company have gathered together. What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"* (16:11). The grumbling at Aaron is against the Lord.; Psalm 106 names the same event with an inner word: *"When men in the camp were jealous of Moses and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord, the earth opened and swallowed up Dathan, and covered the company of Abiram"* (Psa 106:16–17).; Moses himself is *"very angry"* (16:15). The rebels are judged (16:31–35). The next day *"all the congregation of the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and against Aaron, saying, 'You have killed the people of the Lord'"* (16:41). A plague begins, and Aaron *"stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped"* (16:48).; Then God settles it with the staffs: *"And the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout. Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against you"* (17:5). The grumbling is against Moses and Aaron, and God calls it *"from me"*. In v10 it is *"their grumblings against me"*. The staff is kept *"as a sign for the rebels, that you may make an end of their grumblings against me, lest they die"* (17:10).; The grumbling turns to terror: *"Behold, we perish, we are undone, we are all undone. Everyone who comes near … shall die. Are we all to perish?"* (17:12–13).; "Grumble" is *lûn* (H3885B). The verse shows it as spoken complaint. I read the inner side from the passage: the seeking of the priesthood (16:10), and the jealousy that Psalm 106:16 names.

19642.text: What others do around a choice, in these verses: grumble against the chosen man, and God counts it as against himself (Num 16:11; 17:5, 10); seek more than they were given, and are jealous (Num 16:10; Psa 106:16); name a choice as shame, and are angry at what it costs them (1Sa 20:30–31); despise the chosen in the heart, by the eyes of people (2Sa 6:16, 20); despise and abhor the chosen servant (Isa 49:7); conclude from the chosen people's ruin that God rejected them, and despise them in their own sight (Jer 33:24); ask to share the joy of the chosen (Psa 106:5); not know God, and still be called and equipped for the sake of the chosen (Isa 45:4–5); offer an inner act, the humbling of the soul, that God's choosing weighs and does not accept (Isa 58:3–5)

19653.text: Isaiah 1:29 — "the oaks that you desired … the gardens that you have chosen": The oracle opens as a lawsuit: *"Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth"* (v2). The charge goes to the inner being: *"Children have I reared and brought up, but they have rebelled against me"* (v2); *"The ox knows its owner … but Israel does not know, my people do not understand"* (v3); *"The whole head is sick, and the whole heart faint"* (v5); Their worship goes on, and the Lord refuses it: *"I do not delight in the blood of bulls"* (v11); *"your appointed feasts my soul hates"* (v14); *"even though you make many prayers, I will not listen"* (v15).; Then the choice is laid before them, in the same two-sided shape as Isa 7:15: *"cease to do evil, learn to do good"* (v16–17); *"Come now, let us reason together"*, with the offer that sins *"like scarlet"* shall be *"as white as snow"* (v18); the two outcomes: *"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"*; *"but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword"* (v19–20); Being willing, and refusing (here H3985, a different word from Isa 7), are the two sides of the choice. Eating, and being eaten, are its two outcomes.; The oracle ends with those who did not take the offer. v29–31 is figurative speech, and the figure is the point: *"they shall be ashamed of the oaks that you desired; and you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen"*; *"you shall be like an oak whose leaf withers, and like a garden without water"*; *"the strong shall become tinder, and his work a spark, and both of them shall burn together"*; The things they desired and chose become the picture of what they themselves become. They chose oaks and gardens, and they become a withering oak and a garden with no water. The choice comes back as an image of the chooser. The last line goes further: the strong man’s own *"work"* is the spark that sets him alight. What he made burns him, *"with none to quench them"*.; Shame comes first in the verse: *"ashamed"*, *"blush"* (H0954, H2659). The chooser is ashamed of the very thing that was desired and chosen. What drew the desire becomes the cause of the shame.

19660.text: The choice is laid out as an offer, with both outcomes (Isa 1:16–20). *"cease to do evil, learn to do good"*; *"willing"* or *"refuse"*; eat, or be eaten. In Isa 7:15 the right choice also ends in eating.

19667.text: Isaiah 56:4 — "who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant": The foreigners are described in inner terms as well: they *"join themselves to the Lord, to minister to him, to love the name of the Lord, and to be his servants"* (v6). Love of the name stands with the keeping and the holding fast.; What follows in the chapter is the opposite. Israel's own watchmen *"are all without knowledge"*. They are *"shepherds who have no understanding; they have all turned to their own way, each to his own gain"* (v10–11). "Their own way" is the same phrase as in Isaiah 66:3, *"These have chosen their own ways"* (H1870G). The outsiders who choose what the Lord delights in are brought in. The insiders turn to their own way.

19678.text: Deuteronomy 23:16 — "in the place that he shall choose … wherever it suits him": The law concerns *"a slave who has escaped from his master to you"*. Israel is told *"You shall not give up to his master"* (v15). Then the choice is handed to the slave: *"He shall dwell with you, in your midst, in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him"* (v16).; The man who escaped had no say over where he lived. The law gives it back to him. The choice is his, and its ground is his own good: *"wherever it suits him"* is literally "in what is good to him" (H2896A). Israel's part is to honour it: not to hand him back, and not to *"wrong him"* (H3238, to oppress).; The phrase is a weighty one in Deuteronomy. *"the place that he shall choose within one of your towns"* has the same shape as the phrase Deuteronomy uses for the Lord’s own choosing: *"the place that the Lord your God will choose out of all your tribes"* (12:5); *"the place that the Lord will choose in one of your tribes"* (12:14). The words (place, that, choose, in one of your …) are the same (H4725, H0977). I read this as the law giving the escaped slave, in his own small measure, the kind of choosing the Lord keeps for his own dwelling. The verse does not draw the comparison.

19683.text: Acts 15:22, 25 — "it seemed good … having come to one accord, to choose men": The choosing ends a dispute that went to the heart of the faith. Some taught *"Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved"* (v1), and there was *"no small dissension and debate"* (v2).; At the council the first word about choosing is God's. Peter says *"Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe"* (v7). It is the same verb as the church's later choosing (G1586). He goes on: *"God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit … having cleansed their hearts by faith"* (v8–9). The assembly *"fell silent"* and *"listened"* (v12). James gives his judgement from the prophets (v13–21).; Then the church chooses: *"it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch"* (v22). The letter says how they came to it: *"it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men and send them to you"* (v25). "One accord" (G3661) is a single shared mind. The same verb for "seemed good" (G1380) then joins them to the Spirit: *"it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us"* (v28).; So the church's choosing: follows God's choosing, in the same verb; follows listening in silence; comes from one accord; is joined to what seemed good to the Holy Spirit; The outcome is in the hearers' hearts: *"when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement"* (v31). Judas and Silas *"encouraged and strengthened the brothers"* (v32), and were *"sent off in peace"* (v33). The letter answers the *"unsettling"* of their *"minds"* (v24).

19719.text: Israel and election: "Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened" (Rom 11:7); "as regards election, they are beloved for the sake of their forefathers" (Rom 11:28)

19794.text: Face: Choice held open between living and dying (v2); Who: person; Circumstance in the verses: "which I shall choose I cannot tell"; Verses: Phili 1:22

19820.text: 8.4 Route C: assessed here, kept out of the narrative (14): Exo 14:7 ("chosen chariots"); Judg 20:15 ("chosen men"); Judg 20:16 ("chosen men"); Judg 20:34 ("chosen men"); 1Sa 24:2 ("chosen men"); 1Sa 26:2 ("chosen men"); 2Sa 6:1 ("chosen men"); 1Ki 12:21 ("chosen warriors"); 2Ch 11:1 ("chosen warriors"); 2Ch 13:3 ("chosen men"); 2Ch 13:17 ("chosen men"); 2Ch 25:5 ("choice men"); Pro 8:19 ("choice silver"); Song 5:15 ("choice as the cedars").; The other "men selected" verses are route B, because a person's act of choosing is stated. Examples are Exo 17:9 "Choose for us men", 2Sa 10:9 "he chose some of the best men", and the church's choosing in Acts.

19835.text: H0977, "choose". This is the ordinary verb, and it carries most of these verses. The ESV renders it in several ways: *"choose"*; *"desire"*: *"all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (2Sa 19:38); *"to be chosen"* in the sense of preferred: *"To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver"* (Pro 16:16); The same verb is used of the Lord choosing the place for his name (Deu 12:5, 14), and of the Lord's answering choice: *"I also will choose harsh treatment for them"* (Isa 66:4).

19839.text: Choosing has two sides: Refusing is itself choosing. The child *"knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (Isa 7:15). The oracle around that verse shows refusing going both ways. Ahaz refuses the Lord's offer of a sign with pious words: *"I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test"* (Isa 7:12). The people *"refused the waters of Shiloah that flow gently"* (8:6). The right refusing and the wrong refusing are set in one oracle, each with its own consequence.; Not answering is already choosing. *"when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in"* (Isa 65:12; repeated in 66:4). The choosing of what the Lord does not delight in is where the not-listening ends up.; The choice is laid out with both its sides and both its ends: *"cease to do evil, learn to do good"*; *"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"*; *"but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword"* (Isa 1:16–20).

19855.text: Choosing before a God who has already acted: In these verses the human choice is never the first move.; At Shechem it comes after eleven verses of what the Lord did, beginning with *"I took your father Abraham from beyond the River"* (Jos 24:3).; In Isaiah 65 the wrong choice is made in front of a God who says *"Here I am, here I am"* and *"I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people"* (65:1–2).; At the Jerusalem council the church's choosing follows Peter's word that *"God made a choice among you"* (Act 15:7), in the same verb.

19858.text: A choice that is honoured: Choosing is a freedom a person can lose, and Scripture gives it back. The escaped slave *"shall dwell with you … in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him"* (Deu 23:16). The king hands the choice to the man who fed him in the wilderness: *"all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (2Sa 19:38).; The phrase *"the place that he shall choose within one of your towns"* has the same wording as *"the place that the Lord your God will choose"* (Deu 12:5, 14). I read this as the law giving the slave a small share of the kind of choosing the Lord keeps for his own dwelling. The verse does not draw this comparison (open item).

19915.text: 1Ch 28:9 | 10.7 v17 *Willing* quotes "serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind" | Carried since #1986.

19921.text: 3.3 Jer 8:3, in Ch 2 *Wanting to die*: After the Jer 8:3 sentence (fixed under #1991), add: > It is said as part of a judgment the Lord declares. Before it, the bones of the dead are spread *"before the sun and the moon and all the host of heaven, which they have loved and served, which they have gone after"* (8:2). The verse does not say that the one leads to the other.

19940.text: Grumbling, and seeking more. When God's choice of Aaron was challenged, Moses named what lay under it: *"would you seek the priesthood also?"* (Num 16:10). The grumbling at Aaron was against God: *"What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"* (16:11), and God calls it *"the grumblings … which they grumble against you"*, to be made to *"cease from me"* (17:5). Psalm 106 names the inner act: *"men in the camp were jealous of Moses and Aaron"* (Psa 106:16). God's reply was to make the choice plain, with the staff that sprouted. Then the grumbling became terror: *"Are we all to perish?"* (Num 17:13).

19956.text: Seeking, and not obtaining. *"Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened"* (Rom 11:7). The rest were seeking. They were given *"eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear"* (11:8). Paul at once refuses the conclusion that this is the end: *"did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means!"* (11:11). The remnant is chosen *"by grace"*, not works (11:5–6). The passage says how the elect were chosen. It does not say why the rest were not.

19957.text: An inner act weighed by what God chooses: In one passage the inner act of the others is itself set against God's choosing. The people fast and ask, *"Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?"* (Isa 58:3). They *"delight to know my ways"* and *"delight to draw near to God"* (58:2). Yet *"in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers"* (58:3). Then: *"Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself?"* (58:5). "Humble himself" is the humbling of the soul, the same words as their own complaint. What God does choose is turned outward: *"to let the oppressed go free"*, *"to share your bread with the hungry"*, *"not to hide yourself from your own flesh"* (58:6–7).; The self-humbling they offered was not wrong in itself. The passage says it stood beside oppression and quarrelling in the same people, and that it was not what he chooses.

20175.text: Pilate. *"Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released for them Barabbas"* (Mar 15:15). He had asked them, *"Why? What evil has he done?"* (15:14), and earlier, *"do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?"* (Joh 18:39). 20216.text: Knowing is not enough. Belshazzar *"knew all this"* and did not humble his heart (Dan 5:22). In the plan set, God *"understands every plan"* (1Ch 28:9). The will set adds that the person's own knowing does not move the will.

20271.text: The held phrasing in 10.7. The working note in 10.7 holds the shared phrasing of Deuteronomy 23:16 (*"in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him"*) and Deuteronomy 12:5, 14. Batch 1 read Deuteronomy 12 in full. The forms of words differ: 12:5 has *"out of all your tribes"*, 12:14 *"in one of your tribes"*, and 23:16 *"within one of your towns"*. In 23:16 the chooser is the escaped slave. The reading does not settle whether the shared phrase is more than a form of words. It stays held.

20285.text: Romans 11:7: "Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened": Paul asks whether God has rejected his people and answers: *"By no means!"* (v1). *"God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew"* (v2). He gives Elijah, who thought he was alone, and God's reply: *"I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal"* (v4). *"So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace. But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works"* (v5–6).; Then v7: *"What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened"*.; The others are *"the rest"*. Two things are said of them: They were seeking (*epizēteō*, G1934) and did not obtain.; They were hardened (*pōroō*, G4456).; The hardening is described from Scripture: *"God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day"* (v8). The giving is God's act (rule 72, A). The eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear are in the human inner being.; Paul does not leave it there: *"So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous"* (v11). He goes on: *"how much more will their full inclusion mean!"* (v12).

20287.text: 1 Thessalonians 1:4: "For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you": Paul writes of what he remembers of them: *"your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ"* (v3). Then: *"For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you, because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction"* (v4–5).; "Know" is *oida* (G6063). Here another person knows that someone has been chosen. The ESV joins v4 to v5 with "because": the knowing rests on how the gospel came to them. The passage goes on to what was seen in them: *"you received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit"* (v6); *"you became an example to all the believers"* (v7); *"your faith in God has gone forth everywhere"* (v8); *"you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven"* (v9–10)

20291.text: 1 Peter 2:4: "a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious": The chapter opens with what the readers are to put away and to long for: *"So put away all malice and all deceit and hypocrisy and envy and all slander. Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk"* (v1–2).; Then: *"As you come to him, a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious"* (v4).; Two measures stand in one verse: *"rejected by men"* and *"in the sight of God chosen"*. "Rejected" is *apodokimazō* (G0593), to reject after testing. The quotation in v7 uses the same word: *"The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone"*.; The readers share the same name: *"you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation"* (v9). They will be spoken against in turn: *"when they speak against you as evildoers"* (v12).

20293.text: 2 John 1: "The elder to the elect lady and her children, whom I love in truth": *"The elder to the elect lady and her children, whom I love in truth, and not only I, but also all who know the truth, because of the truth that abides in us and will be with us forever"* (v1–2).; The love is the elder's, and it is shared by *"all who know the truth"*. "Love" is *agapaō* (G0025). "Know" is *ginōskō* (G1097). Both are toward the one called elect. The verse grounds the love *"in truth"* and *"because of the truth that abides in us"*. It does not ground it in the choosing.; The letter goes on: *"I rejoiced greatly to find some of your children walking in the truth"* (v4), and *"this is love, that we walk according to his commandments"* (v6).; The HIB/qualifier file has the relation as "none". The reading agrees that the love is not bound to the choosing. "Elect" names the reader.

20452.text: Where they seem to agree (Claude's reading, worth testing).: Thought isn't simply self-authored.; Science: most processing is automatic and unconscious. Predictive-processing models describe the brain as constantly generating expectations before we are aware of them.; Philosophy: phenomenology observes that thoughts arrive rather than being made.; Bible: the heart runs deeper than we can see into. Jeremiah 17:9–10 says the heart is beyond knowing except by God, and in Psalm 139:23 the psalmist asks God to "know my thoughts."; Thought is shaped by what it takes in and dwells on.; Science: neuroplasticity. Repeated patterns strengthen connections.; Philosophy: Vygotsky's view that language and culture are internalised.; Bible: Proverbs 4:23 (guard the heart), Romans 12:2 (be transformed by the renewing of the mind) and Philippians 4:8 (think on these things).

20455.text: 4. Knowing a thought is separate from producing it. 1 Corinthians 2:11 says only "the spirit of that person" knows a person's thoughts, and only God's Spirit knows God's. Separately, God searches and knows human thoughts (Psalm 139:23; 1 Chronicles 28:9; Psalm 94:11; 1 Corinthians 3:20), and so does Jesus (Luke 5:22, 6:8, 11:17; Matthew 9:4, 12:25).: *Caveat:* in 1 Corinthians 2:11 the Strong's number is G3588, the Greek article. The word "thoughts" is supplied by the translation; the Greek says "the things of a person."

H2803G (19 rows) describes craftsmanship: cherubim "skillfully worked" (Exod 26:1, 31) and "skilled design" (Exod 39:3). 20580.text: In Mat 7:8 'asks' is a present participle ('everyone who asks'): the act is anyone's own request, the first of three acts in the series ask, seek, knock, and it is answered by 'receives'.

20581.text: G0154 aiteo, 'asks': to request something from another. In this passage it is the request of a petitioner to a giver, as in 7:9 'if his son asks him for bread'.

20582.text: 'everyone' makes the statement of 7:8 hold for each asker: no person or condition is named that would exclude any.

20583.text: G3956 pas, 'everyone': each one, all; here in the nominative with the participle 'who asks'.

20584.text: 'receives' is what asking yields in 7:8: the asker takes what is given. The verse does not name the giver.

20585.text: G2983 lambano, 'receives': to take or get; here to get what was asked, answering 7:7 'it will be given to you'.

20586.text: In 7:8 'seeks' is the second act of the series and is answered by 'finds'; the verse does not name what is sought.

20587.text: G2212 zeteo, 'seeks': to look for, to search for something. Here it is the seeker's own pursuit, answered by finding.

20588.text: 'finds' is what seeking yields in 7:8: the seeker comes upon what was sought.

20589.text: G2147 heurisko, 'finds': to find, to come upon what was looked for.

20590.text: 'knocks' is the third act of the series in 7:8 and is answered by 'opened'; the verse does not say at what, or who answers.

20591.text: G2925 krouo, 'knocks': to strike, as at a door to be let in.

20592.text: 'it will be opened' is a passive: the opening is done by one the verse does not name, and it answers the knocking.

20593.text: G0455 anoigo, 'opened': to open; in the passive, to be opened, here to the one who knocks.

20594.text: What the three answers give the three acts in Mat 7:8: 'receives' gives asking its result of being given, 'finds' gives seeking its result of coming upon, 'opened' gives knocking its result of being let in; each act has its own answer.

20595.text: 'For' in Mat 7:8 gives the ground of the commands of 7:7: it says why asking, seeking and knocking are to be done. It has no inner-being bearing of its own.

20596.text: The two 'and' in Mat 7:8 join the three clauses of asking, seeking and knocking; they have no inner-being bearing of their own.

20889.text: Joseph is the one seeking; the man who found him is the one who asks about it.

20890.text: Joseph has been sent by Israel to see how his brothers fare (Gen 37:14) and is alone when the man finds him.

20891.text: A man who came upon Joseph asked him what he was seeking.

20892.text: Joseph is taken to be seeking something; the question assumes it.

20893.text: Joseph is found wandering about; the man then asks what he seeks.

20894.text: The question draws out the seeking that the verse has not yet named.

20895.text: Discovery: what Joseph is seeking is not stated in this verse; the passage gives it.

21296.text: Being silent is a person's, or God's, holding back of speech for a reason the verse shows: submission, fear, shame, awe, wisdom, obedience, waiting, or failure to speak up; or the refusal of it (anguish, praise, the watchmen's duty).

21301.text: Call is a purposeful act of the inner being turned to God: calling or crying out to the Lord, or on his name, in need, trust, praise or worship, or refusing to.

21308.text: Call is here the judgement a person puts on a thing in naming it (calling evil good, the Sabbath a delight, a fast acceptable): a valuing of the heart voiced in speech.

21311.text: Called here only names, designates or labels a person, place or thing (to be called such a name, to call it so); no inner-being operation is voiced by it.

21313.text: Called is here the outward act of summoning, addressing or sending for another person or thing; it bears on the other's response but names no inner-being operation of the one who calls.

21314.text: Called is the standing given by God's call (the vocation); it is what diligence, worthiness or walking is directed at, not an inner operation in itself.

21315.text: Called is God's own act of summoning, choosing or appointing a person or people; it bears on their inner response (faith, obedience, hope), which other words of the verse name, and is the outward act upon them.

21318.text: Called is here the cry or call of a person to another in need or appeal: a purposeful voicing of the person's own need, longing or request.

21325.text: Calling here only names, designates or labels a person, place or thing (to be called such a name, to call it so); no inner-being operation is voiced by it.

21366.text: Offered is here an offering made to God in a stated inner condition (thanksgiving, joy, faith, fear, trust, willingness, resolve, cost, weeping, reverence or conscience), or refused for want of it; the act bears on that condition, which other words of the verse name.

21386.text: Old here states an age, an old age or an age class (years old, an old man, young and old, the older brother); no inner-being operation is voiced by it.

21390.text: Old here dates a thing to the past (of old, the days of old, from of old) or names the people or prophets of old; no inner-being operation is voiced by it.

21407.text: Anger is here the anger, wrath or fury of God against persons or nations (kindled, poured out, turned away, executed, provoked); it is God's own act upon them, and bears on their inner response, which other words of the verse name, if at all.

21408.text: Anger is here the anger, wrath, rage or fury of a person or people: a state of the heart aroused against another, a thing or God, named by the word itself.

21410.text: Angry is here the anger, wrath, rage or fury of a person or people: a state of the heart aroused against another, a thing or God, named by the word itself.

21411.text: Angry is here the anger, wrath or fury of God against persons or nations (kindled, poured out, turned away, executed, provoked); it is God's own act upon them, and bears on their inner response, which other words of the verse name, if at all.

21424.text: Madness is here madness or derangement of the mind or heart: a state of the inner being, set against wisdom or sanity, or a craze such as a passion for idols.

21434.text: Wrath is here the anger, wrath or fury of God against persons or nations (kindled, poured out, turned away, executed, provoked); it is God's own act upon them, and bears on their inner response, which other words of the verse name, if at all.

21450.text: Godly gives a moral condition to what it binds (an upright heart, a righteous or wicked way, godly grief, walking uprightly, a sinful nation): the uprightness, godliness or wickedness of the heart, speech, way or conduct.

21458.text: Holy here names an attribute of God or of his rule (a righteous Lord, the scepter of uprightness, the Holy One, his holy name or Spirit, the mystery of godliness); no operation of a person's inner being is voiced by it.

21459.text: Holy here is the holiness or sacredness of a place, day, offering, oil, writing or thing set apart (a holy place, a sacred gift, the holy mountain); no inner-being operation is voiced by it.

21470.text: Righteous is here the godly, the righteous, the upright, the wicked or the ungodly as a class of persons toward whom an act is directed or whom an event befalls (the Lord keeps the godly, do not envy the wicked, Christ died for the ungodly); the act is named by another word of the verse.

21471.text: Righteous gives a moral condition to what it binds (an upright heart, a righteous or wicked way, godly grief, walking uprightly, a sinful nation): the uprightness, godliness or wickedness of the heart, speech, way or conduct.

21472.text: Righteous is here God's own righteous, upright or holy act toward persons (judging, vindicating, saving, delivering); it is the outward act upon them and bears on their inner response, named by other words of the verse.

21477.text: Righteousness is here the godliness, devoutness, reverence or uprightness of a person as a state of the heart toward God or toward what is right (a devout man who feared God, godliness trained and pursued, uprightness of heart, reverence and awe).

21478.text: Righteousness is here God's own righteous, upright or holy act toward persons (judging, vindicating, saving, delivering); it is the outward act upon them and bears on their inner response, named by other words of the verse.

21494.text: Upright is here the godly, the righteous, the upright, the wicked or the ungodly as a class of persons toward whom an act is directed or whom an event befalls (the Lord keeps the godly, do not envy the wicked, Christ died for the ungodly); the act is named by another word of the verse.

21495.text: Upright is here the godliness, devoutness, reverence or uprightness of a person as a state of the heart toward God or toward what is right (a devout man who feared God, godliness trained and pursued, uprightness of heart, reverence and awe).

21499.text: Uprightly gives a moral condition to what it binds (an upright heart, a righteous or wicked way, godly grief, walking uprightly, a sinful nation): the uprightness, godliness or wickedness of the heart, speech, way or conduct.

21503.text: Wicked is here the godly, the righteous, the upright, the wicked or the ungodly as a class of persons toward whom an act is directed or whom an event befalls (the Lord keeps the godly, do not envy the wicked, Christ died for the ungodly); the act is named by another word of the verse.

21504.text: Wicked gives a moral condition to what it binds (an upright heart, a righteous or wicked way, godly grief, walking uprightly, a sinful nation): the uprightness, godliness or wickedness of the heart, speech, way or conduct.

21505.text: Wicked is here the wickedness, ungodliness or sinfulness of a person as a state or practice of the heart, set against godliness and what is right (ungodliness, a heart busy with iniquity, a wicked deed, sinful passions).

21508.text: Wickedness is here the wickedness, ungodliness or sinfulness of a person as a state or practice of the heart, set against godliness and what is right (ungodliness, a heart busy with iniquity, a wicked deed, sinful passions).

21517.text: Choose here is God's choosing of a place, city, house or thing, or his own sovereign will over things (the place the Lord will choose, the city I have chosen, a body as he has chosen, the Lord is my chosen portion); no operation of a person's inner being is voiced by it.

21526.text: Chosen here describes the excellence of a thing, or persons or things selected as the best (choice silver, the choicest cedars, chosen warriors, 700 chosen men); no inner-being operation is voiced by it.

21541.text: Above names the realm that is the object of the inner operation: the things above are what the mind is to seek and set itself on.

21542.text: Above here is a place or position in space, a rank or a comparison of things, people or God; no human inner-being operation is qualified by it.

21543.text: Altogether gives completeness to the inner state it is joined to: shame in full, vanity through and through.

21545.text: Arise gives rousing to the inner operation it joins: doubts coming up in the heart, the sluggard roused from sleep, the heart roused to pray, the sleeper called up from deadness, a resolve acted on.

21550.text: Awake names the inner operation of staying alert or being roused: the watchfulness of the servants who wait, the sober watching asked of believers, the rousing from sleep or drunkenness, the rousing of one's own glory to praise.

21563.text: Complaint here is a legal charge or accusation, not an inner operation.

21566.text: Devise names the inner operation of planning, scheming or designing: evil devised in the heart, good devised, and the skill given to devise designs.

21597.text: High gives loftiness to the proud heart and its ways (the high hand, the horn lifted on high, the high door, the nest set on high, the high tree brought low), or places the wise and the known beyond reach (too high for a fool, too high to attain).

21599.text: High here is a measure of height, a high place, a high priest, God on high or a high social rank; no human inner-being operation is named or qualified.

21626.text: Means here is by no means, by all means, resources (according to their means) or what a word means; no inner-being operation is named or qualified.

21627.text: Misconduct here is the accusation of shameful behaviour laid against a wife; an outward deed charged, no inner operation named or qualified.

21641.text: Put names an act on the inner being: God puts wisdom into the mind, earnest care into the heart, eternity into the heart, a spirit in a man, dread on the peoples; Timothy is to be put at ease.

21642.text: Put here is placing, setting, laying or appointing a thing, a person, a name or a garrison, or putting someone in prison or on the sword; no inner-being operation is named or qualified.

21645.text: Put here is placing, setting, laying, putting on or appointing a thing, a garment, a person or a hook, or putting someone in prison; no inner-being operation is named or qualified.

21680.text: Stature here is bodily height or growth; no inner-being operation is qualified.

21690.text: Surround here is encircling by walls, soldiers, enemies, or God; no inner-being operation is named or qualified.

21698.text: Treat here is how one deals with a servant, a sister or a people; an outward way of dealing, the inner disposition is named by another word.

21699.text: Treated here is how a person was dealt with, kindly or shamefully; an outward way of dealing, the inner disposition is named by another word.

21705.text: Used here is employed, accustomed or spoken (a proverb, a curse, a vessel, divination); no inner-being operation is named or qualified.

21709.text: Walk here is bodily walking, or the course of conduct (walk in his ways, statutes or customs); the walk itself is outward conduct, no inner-being operation is named or qualified in it.

21711.text: Walk here is bodily walking, or the course of conduct (walk in his ways, statutes or the light); the walk itself is outward conduct, no inner-being operation is named or qualified in it.

21718.text: Weight here is the weight of metal, a measure, a crown, a pillar, or the weight of glory; no inner operation is named or qualified.

21732.text: Young here is youth in age, a young man, woman, animal or offspring; a description of age or kind, no inner-being operation is named or qualified.

how_to_fill: evaluations: one for each surface item (vl_id); observations: one for each surface and role; existing: an action for each existing observation (accept, modify, delete, merge, leave). See USER-GUIDE section 8.18.
